guides.title: Rocks, Minerals & the Rock Cycle
guides.summary: What minerals and rocks actually are, how to identify them by hardness, streak, cleavage and acid fizz, the three rock families, and how the rock cycle continuously converts each into the others.

sections.heading: First principles: element, mineral, rock
sections.body:
A MINERAL is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and an ordered internal atomic arrangement (a crystal lattice). All four conditions must hold. Glacier ice qualifies; liquid water does not (no lattice); coal does not (organic); steel does not (man-made). A ROCK is a naturally occurring aggregate of one or more minerals, plus sometimes volcanic glass or organic matter. Granite is a rock built from at least three minerals — quartz, feldspar and mica. Quartz is a mineral: SiO₂, everywhere, always.
CRUSTAL ABUNDANCE (percent by mass): oxygen 46.6, silicon 27.7, aluminium 8.1, iron 5.0, calcium 3.6, sodium 2.8, potassium 2.6, magnesium 2.1. Because O and Si dominate, about 92% of crustal minerals are SILICATES, built from the silica tetrahedron: one Si⁴⁺ ion surrounded by four O²⁻ ions, written (SiO₄)⁴⁻. Tetrahedra bond by sharing corner oxygen atoms, and how many corners they share defines the mineral class:
• 0 shared — isolated tetrahedra → olivine, (Mg,Fe)₂SiO₄
• 2 shared — single chains → pyroxene (augite)
• 2–3 shared — double chains → amphibole (hornblende)
• 3 shared — sheets → micas (biotite, muscovite) and clays
• 4 shared — frameworks → quartz SiO₂ and the feldspars (KAlSi₃O₈, NaAlSi₃O₈, CaAl₂Si₂O₈)
More sharing means a higher Si:O ratio, a lighter-coloured and lower-density mineral, and a lower melting temperature. Non-silicate classes worth knowing: carbonates (calcite CaCO₃, dolomite CaMg(CO₃)₂), oxides (hematite Fe₂O₃, magnetite Fe₃O₄), sulphides (pyrite FeS₂, galena PbS), sulphates (gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O), halides (halite NaCl) and native elements (gold, graphite, diamond).

sections.heading: Identifying a mineral: seven field tests in order
sections.body:
Run these in sequence on a fresh (unweathered) surface. You need only a pocket knife, a copper coin, a streak plate (unglazed porcelain tile, or the back of a bathroom tile), a magnet and dilute vinegar or 5% hydrochloric acid.
1. LUSTRE — metallic (looks like polished metal: pyrite, galena, magnetite) or non-metallic (glassy/vitreous like quartz, pearly like mica, earthy like limonite, resinous, silky). This is the single biggest first split.
2. STREAK — drag the specimen hard across the unglazed tile. The colour of the POWDER is far more reliable than the colour of the lump. Hematite is silver-black or red as a lump but always leaves a red-brown streak; pyrite looks gold but streaks greenish-black — this one test separates "fool's gold" from gold, which streaks golden yellow. Minerals harder than about 7 will not streak (they scratch the plate instead).
3. HARDNESS — Mohs scale, a purely ordinal ranking of scratch resistance: 1 talc, 2 gypsum, 3 calcite, 4 fluorite, 5 apatite, 6 orthoclase feldspar, 7 quartz, 8 topaz, 9 corundum, 10 diamond. It is NOT linear — diamond is roughly 4 times harder than corundum in absolute indentation terms. Field references: fingernail ≈ 2.5, copper coin ≈ 3.5, steel knife or nail ≈ 5.5, glass ≈ 5.5, steel file ≈ 6.5, quartz ≈ 7. Test by trying to scratch the unknown with a known, then reverse it; wipe the mark to check you have made a groove and not just left metal smear.
4. CLEAVAGE vs. FRACTURE — cleavage is breakage along planes of weak atomic bonding, producing flat, repeatable, reflective faces. Count the directions and note the angles: mica = 1 direction (peels into sheets); feldspar = 2 at about 90°; pyroxene = 2 at about 87°/93°; amphibole = 2 at about 56°/124° (this angle is the classic way to tell hornblende from augite); halite and galena = 3 at 90° (cubes); calcite = 3 NOT at 90° (rhombs). Fracture is breakage with no planar weakness: quartz shows conchoidal (shell-like, curved) fracture.
5. ACID TEST — a drop of dilute HCl or strong vinegar on calcite fizzes vigorously (CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑). Dolomite fizzes only when powdered or warmed. Nothing else common fizzes, so this instantly identifies limestone and marble.
6. MAGNETISM — magnetite is strongly magnetic; pyrrhotite weakly so.
7. SPECIFIC GRAVITY — heft it. Quartz has SG ≈ 2.65 (normal-feeling); galena SG 7.6 and gold SG 19.3 feel startlingly heavy for their size. SG = (density of the mineral) ÷ (density of water at 4 °C, 1000 kg/m³), so it is a dimensionless number.

sections.heading: Igneous rocks: crystallised melt
sections.body:
IGNEOUS rocks solidify from molten silicate liquid — MAGMA below ground, LAVA above. They are classified on two independent axes.
AXIS 1, TEXTURE (= cooling rate): Slow cooling at depth grows large, interlocking, visible crystals — PHANERITIC or intrusive/plutonic (granite, diorite, gabbro). Fast cooling at the surface gives crystals too small to see — APHANITIC or extrusive/volcanic (rhyolite, andesite, basalt). Instant quenching gives no crystals at all — glassy obsidian. Gas-frothed lava gives vesicular pumice (so full of bubbles it floats, bulk density under 1000 kg/m³) and scoria. Two-stage cooling gives PORPHYRITIC texture: big phenocrysts floating in a fine groundmass, which tells you the magma sat in a chamber and then erupted. Explosive fragmentation gives pyroclastic tuff.
AXIS 2, COMPOSITION (= silica content): felsic 65–75% SiO₂ (light-coloured, quartz + K-feldspar, density ≈ 2700 kg/m³) → granite/rhyolite; intermediate 55–65% → diorite/andesite; mafic 45–55% SiO₂ (dark, pyroxene + Ca-plagioclase + olivine, density ≈ 3000 kg/m³) → gabbro/basalt; ultramafic under 45% → peridotite, the rock of the mantle.
BOWEN'S REACTION SERIES states the order in which minerals crystallise as magma cools from about 1250 °C to 650 °C. The discontinuous (ferromagnesian) branch runs olivine → pyroxene → amphibole → biotite; the continuous (plagioclase) branch runs Ca-rich → Na-rich; both converge on K-feldspar → muscovite → quartz last. Two enormous consequences follow. First, FRACTIONAL CRYSTALLISATION: if early-formed olivine and pyroxene crystals settle out of a basaltic magma, the remaining liquid becomes progressively richer in silica — one parent magma can produce a whole range of rocks. Second, the GOLDICH WEATHERING SERIES is Bowen's run backwards: minerals that formed at the highest temperature and farthest from surface conditions weather fastest. Olivine rots quickly; quartz, which crystallises last and lowest, survives — which is exactly why beach and desert sand is overwhelmingly quartz.

sections.heading: Sedimentary rocks: the archive of the surface
sections.body:
SEDIMENTARY rocks form at ordinary surface temperatures and pressures, and they hold essentially all the fossils and all the fuel. They come in three genetic kinds.
CLASTIC (detrital) rocks are made of transported fragments, and are named by GRAIN SIZE on the Wentworth scale: clay under 0.004 mm → claystone/shale; silt 0.004–0.0625 mm → siltstone; sand 0.0625–2 mm → sandstone; granule/pebble/cobble/boulder above 2 mm → conglomerate if the clasts are rounded, breccia if angular. Two textural properties read the transport history directly. ROUNDNESS increases with distance travelled, because corners abrade first — angular clasts mean a short trip. SORTING is the spread of grain sizes: a well-sorted sandstone (all grains alike) means a persistent, selective agent such as wind or surf; a poorly sorted mixture of clay through boulders means a non-selective dump such as a glacier (till) or a debris flow. So an angular, poorly sorted breccia says "very local, very fast"; a rounded, well-sorted quartz sandstone says "long journey, high energy, repeatedly reworked".
CHEMICAL rocks precipitate from solution: limestone (CaCO₃), rock salt (halite, NaCl), gypsum, chert (microcrystalline SiO₂). Evaporation of seawater precipitates minerals in a fixed order as concentration rises — calcite first (at about 50% volume loss), then gypsum (about 80%), then halite (about 90%), then bitter potassium and magnesium salts. Finding that sequence in a core tells you a sea basin dried up.
BIOCHEMICAL/ORGANIC rocks are built by life: most limestone is accumulated shell and coral debris; chalk is a limestone of microscopic coccolith plates; coal is compressed plant matter (peat → lignite → bituminous → anthracite, with carbon rising from about 60% to over 90% as water and volatiles are pressed out).
LITHIFICATION turns loose sediment into rock by (1) COMPACTION — burial pressure squeezing out pore water, reducing the porosity of mud from about 60% to under 10%, and (2) CEMENTATION — groundwater precipitating calcite, silica or iron oxide in the remaining pores. Sedimentary rocks are the only ones that preserve BEDDING (layering), cross-bedding (which records current direction), ripple marks, mud cracks, raindrop impressions, burrows and body fossils.

sections.heading: Metamorphic rocks: solid-state rebuilding
sections.body:
METAMORPHISM is the change of a pre-existing rock (the protolith) into a new one by heat, pressure and chemically active fluids, WITHOUT melting. The working range is roughly 150–200 °C at the low end (below that it is diagenesis) up to about 850 °C at the high end (above that the rock partially melts and you get migmatite, then igneous rock). Pressure is stated in kilobars: 1 kbar ≈ 100 MPa ≈ the pressure at about 3.5 km depth in the crust.
Types: CONTACT (thermal) metamorphism is high temperature, low pressure, in a halo around an intruding pluton — it makes non-foliated rocks such as hornfels and marble. REGIONAL (dynamothermal) metamorphism is high T and high directed pressure across whole mountain belts — it makes foliated rocks. BURIAL, HYDROTHERMAL and SHOCK (meteorite impact) metamorphism are the other varieties.
FOLIATION is the parallel alignment of platy or elongate minerals perpendicular to the maximum compressive stress. Its progressive development defines the classic grade sequence from a shale protolith: SLATE (very fine, splits into flat sheets, ~200 °C) → PHYLLITE (silky sheen as micas grow, ~300 °C) → SCHIST (visible aligned micas, ~450 °C) → GNEISS (coarse light/dark mineral banding, feldspar-rich, ~650 °C). Non-foliated products come from single-mineral protoliths where there is nothing platy to align: limestone → marble; quartz sandstone → quartzite (which breaks THROUGH the grains, not around them — a useful field test); basalt → greenstone/amphibolite.
INDEX MINERALS pin down the conditions, because each is stable only within a known temperature-pressure window: chlorite (low grade) → biotite → garnet → staurolite → kyanite → sillimanite (high grade). The Al₂SiO₅ polymorphs are the neatest example — identical formula, three structures: andalusite forms at low pressure, kyanite at high pressure and moderate temperature, sillimanite at high temperature. Identify which one you have and you have read the burial depth of the rock.

sections.heading: The rock cycle as a mass-balance system
sections.body:
The ROCK CYCLE is the statement that all three rock families are interconvertible and that no path is one-way. The complete set of transitions:
• Magma → (cooling/crystallisation) → igneous rock
• Any rock → (weathering + erosion + transport + deposition + lithification) → sedimentary rock
• Any rock → (heat + pressure, staying solid) → metamorphic rock
• Any rock → (melting above the solidus) → magma
The important non-obvious point is that there are shortcuts: an igneous rock can go straight to metamorphic without ever being a sediment; a metamorphic rock can be weathered straight into sediment; a sedimentary rock can melt directly. The two energy sources driving the whole loop are Earth's internal heat (radioactive decay of ²³⁸U, ²³²Th and ⁴⁰K plus residual accretionary heat, together delivering about 47 terawatts through the surface) which powers the melting and metamorphism, and solar energy (about 174,000 TW intercepted) which powers the water cycle, wind and the weathering-erosion half.
RESIDENCE TIMES make it concrete. Oceanic crust is created at ridges and destroyed at trenches on a cycle of roughly 100–200 million years, so no seafloor older than about 180 Ma exists. Continental crust is buoyant and is not subducted wholesale, so it survives: the oldest intact rocks (Acasta Gneiss, Canada) are about 4.03 billion years old and the oldest known mineral grains (detrital zircons from Jack Hills, Australia) are about 4.4 billion years old — those zircons have been recycled through sandstones repeatedly while the original rock has vanished entirely. Volumetrically, sedimentary rocks form only about 5–8% of the crust by volume but cover about 75% of the land surface — a thin veneer over an igneous and metamorphic basement.
WORKED EXAMPLE — trace one silicon atom. It crystallises into a quartz grain in a granite pluton 5 km down. Uplift and erosion expose the granite; feldspar around the quartz weathers to clay, freeing the grain. A river carries it 400 km, rounding it slightly; it is deposited on a beach, buried to 2 km, and cemented by silica into sandstone. Continental collision buries the sandstone to 20 km and 500 °C, recrystallising it into quartzite. The mountain belt erodes over 50 Ma, exposing the quartzite, which weathers and releases the same grain to a new river. Total elapsed time: several hundred million years, and the atom has occupied all three rock families without ever changing its element.

sections.heading: Practical uses, common mistakes and safety
sections.body:
PRACTICAL VALUE. Knowing the rock under your feet predicts water, stability and resources. Limestone and other carbonates dissolve to form karst — caves, sinkholes and rapid, unfiltered groundwater flow, meaning a spring in limestone country may be bacterially contaminated even if it looks clear. Shale and clay-rich rock hold water but transmit it poorly, make weak slopes, and slide when wet. Granite and quartzite make strong, low-permeability foundations, with water available only from fractures. Sandstone with 15–25% porosity is the classic aquifer and reservoir rock. For construction: quartzite and granite are excellent aggregate; shale is unsuitable (it slakes and crumbles when wetted and dried). For a fire ring, never use river cobbles, sandstone or any porous stone that has been sitting in water — trapped pore water flashes to steam and can spall a rock violently; use dry, dense, non-porous stone and keep people back.
COMMON MISTAKES. (1) Identifying minerals by colour — quartz alone comes in clear, white, pink, purple, smoky and black; use streak and hardness instead. (2) Testing on a weathered surface — always break a fresh face. (3) Confusing cleavage with crystal faces: cleavage repeats indefinitely as you keep breaking the sample; a crystal face is a one-off growth surface. (4) Calling any layered rock "sedimentary" — gneiss is banded and metamorphic; foliation cuts across bedding, whereas bedding is depositional and continuous. (5) Reporting a Mohs number as if it were linear.
SAFETY. Wear eye protection whenever you strike a rock — quartz and obsidian throw glass-sharp flakes. Never hammer directly on a hardened steel hammer face (steel spalls). Treat road cuts and quarry faces as unstable and never work directly beneath an overhang or a fresh vertical face; loose blocks fall without warning, especially after rain or a freeze-thaw night. Use only dilute acid (5% HCl or household vinegar), keep it in a dropper bottle, never carry concentrated acid in the field, and rinse skin immediately with plenty of water if splashed. Avoid inhaling dust from breaking rock — crystalline silica dust causes silicosis, so break rock outdoors, downwind, and wet the surface if you are doing it repeatedly. Some minerals warrant care: galena is lead sulphide (wash hands, never lick a specimen — the old "taste test" for halite is a bad habit), cinnabar contains mercury, and asbestiform amphiboles must never be crushed or inhaled. Finally, check the law: collecting is prohibited in most national parks and on many protected and private lands.

sections.heading: Crystal Systems: Why a Mineral's Shape Isn't an Accident
sections.body: Every mineral is a crystal at heart, even when it never grew a single flat face — its atoms are locked into a repeating three-dimensional lattice, and that internal geometry is what a mineralogist calls a crystal system. There are seven: isometric (cubic), tetragonal, orthorhombic, hexagonal, trigonal, monoclinic, and triclinic, distinguished by the lengths and angles of the unit cell's three (or four, for hexagonal) crystallographic axes. Halite (NaCl) crystallizes isometric because its sodium and chlorine ions pack into a perfect cube, and that's exactly why a chunk of rock salt cleaves into smaller and smaller perfect cubes no matter how many times you split it — you're not cutting the crystal, you're finding the plane of weakest bonding that was always there. Quartz, by contrast, is trigonal: silicon and oxygen spiral around a threefold axis, which is why natural quartz crystals show six-sided prisms capped by pyramidal points, and why quartz has no cleavage at all — the Si-O bonds are so uniformly strong in every direction that it breaks with a curved, glassy conchoidal fracture instead, the same way glass does. Mica sits at the opposite extreme: its sheet-silicate structure bonds atoms tightly within each sheet but only weakly between sheets, giving it one perfect cleavage direction so pronounced you can peel a single crystal into paper-thin, flexible sheets with a fingernail. Calcite's rhombohedral cleavage — three directions, none at 90° — comes straight out of its trigonal carbonate lattice, and it's diagnostic enough that a jeweler's loupe on a broken calcite crystal is often enough to identify it on sight. The general rule worth carrying into the field: cleavage planes are always parallel to the weakest bonds in the lattice, so once you understand roughly how a mineral's atoms are stacked, you can often predict how it will break before you ever hit it with a hammer.

sections.heading: Bowen's Reaction Series: Why Granite and Basalt Never Mix
sections.body: In the 1910s and 1920s, petrologist Norman L. Bowen melted rock powders in a furnace and slow-cooled them under controlled conditions, watching under a microscope which minerals crystallized first and which came last. The pattern he found — Bowen's Reaction Series — has two branches. The discontinuous branch crystallizes a sequence of chemically distinct minerals as the melt cools: olivine first (around 1200°C), then pyroxene, then amphibole, then biotite mica, each forming by the earlier mineral reacting with the remaining melt rather than simply growing alongside it. Running in parallel, the continuous branch crystallizes plagioclase feldspar, whose composition slides smoothly from calcium-rich to sodium-rich as the melt cools. Both branches converge at the bottom on the last minerals to crystallize: potassium feldspar, muscovite mica, and finally quartz, which simply fills whatever space remains. This is why olivine and quartz almost never appear together in the same igneous rock: if leftover silica-rich melt is still present after olivine forms, it reacts with the olivine to make pyroxene rather than letting both minerals coexist — finding them as neighbors is a genuine geological oddity worth noting in a field notebook. The series also explains magmatic differentiation: if early, dense crystals like olivine and pyroxene sink out of a magma chamber before the rock solidifies (fractional crystallization), the remaining melt is driven toward the quartz-and-feldspar end of the series — exactly how a single parent basaltic magma can, over time, produce an entire suite of rocks from gabbro through diorite to granite.

sections.heading: Putting a Clock on the Cycle: Radiometric Dating in Outline
sections.body: The rock cycle describes a direction of change, but it took radioactivity to attach actual numbers to it. Unstable isotopes decay to a daughter isotope at a fixed statistical rate, described by N = N₀e^(−λt); rearranged around the half-life (t½ = ln(2)/λ), this becomes the workhorse dating equation. Uranium-238 decays to lead-206 with a half-life of 4.47 billion years, useful for the oldest rocks on Earth; potassium-40 to argon-40 (1.25 billion years) is the standard for volcanic rocks; rubidium-87 to strontium-87 (48.8 billion years) suits ancient continental crust; and carbon-14 to nitrogen-14, with a half-life of just 5,730 years, is useless for dating rocks directly but invaluable for organic material up to roughly 50,000 years old. A crucial catch: radiometric ages record the last time a mineral cooled below its closure temperature, the point where the crystal lattice becomes tight enough to trap the daughter isotope — so a zircon's uranium-lead date typically marks original crystallization, while a mica's potassium-argon date can instead mark a later metamorphic event that reset its clock. This is also why sedimentary rocks are almost never dated directly: their grains are recycled from older rocks of mixed ages. Instead, geologists date the volcanic ash layers interbedded within a sedimentary sequence and bracket the rock's age between the ash beds above and below it — precisely how boundaries like the 66-million-year Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction line were pinned to real numbers.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: A basic mineral-identification kit costs less than a good field guide and turns the seven field tests from earlier into something you can run on a kitchen table.
ingredients: An unglazed white porcelain streak plate (the back of a bathroom tile works if a proper one isn't at hand) — a hardware store or hobby/rock shop
A steel pocketknife or a geologist's rock pick with a hardened tip, for scratch-hardness testing — a hardware or outdoor-gear store
A small piece of ordinary window glass (hardness ~5.5) and a copper penny (hardness ~3.5), both useful fixed points on the Mohs scale
A strong magnet (a small neodymium disc magnet works well) to test for magnetite and other magnetic minerals — an electronics or hardware store

Dilute hydrochloric acid (about 10%) in a small dropper bottle, for the carbonate fizz test — a rock-and-mineral or science-supply shop; always pair with safety glasses and use outdoors or in ventilated space, since it irritates skin and eyes on contact
A 10x hand lens or jeweler's loupe for examining crystal faces and grain texture — an optics, hobby, or rock-and-mineral shop

A basic Mohs hardness pick set (points of known hardness from 2 to 9) — a rock-and-mineral or geology-supply shop, though the improvised scale of fingernail, penny, knife, and glass covers most everyday identification
A field notebook and small sample bags or an egg carton for keeping specimens separated and labeled

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Identify Five Unknown Specimens Like a Field Geologist
sections.body: The seven field tests only build real skill once you've run them on rocks you didn't already know the answer to — here's a concrete way to do that with whatever you can pick up in a yard, streambed, or gravel driveway.
steps: Collect five different-looking rock or mineral specimens, at least fist-sized if possible, ideally from different locations (a streambed, a gravel driveway, a road cut, a garden bed).
For each specimen, first record color and luster (metallic, glassy, pearly, dull) in your notebook before testing anything — color alone is often misleading, so note it but don't rely on it.
Run the streak test: scrape the specimen firmly across the unglazed porcelain plate and record the color of the powder left behind, not the color of the specimen itself.

Test hardness by attempting to scratch the specimen with your fingernail, then a penny, then the knife blade, then the glass plate, working up in order and recording the highest material that successfully scratches it.

Check for cleavage versus fracture: look for flat, repeating, reflective planes (cleavage) versus curved or irregular broken surfaces (fracture), and count how many distinct cleavage directions you can see.
Apply a single drop of dilute acid to an inconspicuous spot and watch for fizzing, which indicates a carbonate mineral such as calcite; wipe it off afterward and wash your hands.
Test with the magnet to rule in or out magnetite or other strongly magnetic minerals.
Cross-reference your recorded properties against a mineral identification chart or field guide to reach a tentative ID.

Decide whether each specimen is a single mineral or a rock made of several minerals grown together — if you see multiple distinct minerals with your hand lens, classify it as igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic and write a one-line reasoning for your call.

guides.title: Plate Tectonics, Earthquakes & Volcanoes
guides.summary: Earth's interior structure, the mechanics of plate motion, the three boundary types, how earthquakes are measured and how to survive one, and why different volcanoes erupt in fundamentally different ways.

sections.heading: Earth's interior: the layers and how we know
sections.body:
COMPOSITIONAL LAYERS (defined by chemistry):
• CRUST — oceanic crust is basaltic, 5–10 km thick, density ≈ 3000 kg/m³, young (0–180 Ma). Continental crust is granitic on average, 30–50 km thick (up to 70 km under Tibet), density ≈ 2700 kg/m³, up to 4.0 billion years old.
• MANTLE — peridotite (olivine + pyroxene), from the base of the crust to 2890 km depth. It is 84% of Earth's volume and about 67% of its mass. It is SOLID rock that flows plastically over geological time at roughly 10⁻¹⁴ to 10⁻¹⁵ per second strain rate — think of it as extremely stiff toffee, not liquid.
• CORE — iron-nickel alloy with about 10% light elements (S, O, Si), from 2890 km to Earth's centre at 6371 km. The outer core (2890–5150 km) is liquid; the inner core (5150–6371 km) is solid despite being hotter (roughly 5400 °C) because pressure there exceeds 330 GPa.
MECHANICAL LAYERS (defined by how they deform — this is the set that matters for tectonics):
• LITHOSPHERE — crust plus the rigid uppermost mantle, 0–100 km thick under oceans (thickening with age) and up to 200–250 km under old continental cratons. This is what breaks into PLATES.
• ASTHENOSPHERE — 100–350 km, weak and ductile, close to its melting point (perhaps 0.1–1% partial melt), on which the plates slide.
• MESOSPHERE (lower mantle), OUTER CORE, INNER CORE.
HOW WE KNOW: seismic waves. P-waves (primary, compressional, particle motion parallel to travel, about 6 km/s in crust and 13 km/s at the base of the mantle) pass through both solids and liquids. S-waves (secondary, shear, particle motion perpendicular, roughly 0.58 × P-wave speed) cannot propagate through liquid, because a liquid has zero shear modulus. Wave speed follows v_p = √((K + 4µ/3)/ρ) and v_s = √(µ/ρ), where K is the bulk modulus (Pa), µ the shear modulus (Pa) and ρ the density (kg/m³). The S-WAVE SHADOW ZONE — no S-waves arrive beyond 103° of arc from an earthquake — is direct proof the outer core is liquid. The P-wave shadow zone between 103° and 143° is caused by refraction at the core-mantle boundary. Discontinuities in velocity mark the boundaries: the Moho (crust/mantle, discovered 1909), the 410 km and 660 km transition zones (mineral phase changes in olivine), and the Gutenberg discontinuity at 2890 km (mantle/core).

sections.heading: Plate tectonics: the engine
sections.body:
The lithosphere is broken into about 7 major plates (Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic) and a dozen or so minor ones (Nazca, Cocos, Caribbean, Philippine, Arabian, Juan de Fuca, Scotia). They move at 1–15 cm per year — roughly the speed your fingernails grow. Measured directly by GPS since the 1990s and confirmed by seafloor magnetic stripes.
EVIDENCE, historically: (1) Wegener's continental fit, matching Permian Glossopteris flora and Mesosaurus fossils across the Atlantic, and matching mountain belts (Appalachians–Caledonides). (2) Palaeomagnetism — apparent polar wander paths for different continents only reconcile if the continents moved, not the pole. (3) Seafloor spreading — Vine, Matthews and Morley (1963) showed the symmetric magnetic stripes flanking mid-ocean ridges record reversals of Earth's magnetic field, giving both the direction and rate of spreading. (4) Age and sediment thickness of the seafloor both increase away from ridges, and no seafloor is older than about 180 Ma. (5) The Wadati-Benioff zone — earthquakes deepening from a trench inland along a plane dipping 30–60°, imaging the subducting slab down to 700 km.
DRIVING FORCES, in order of importance:
1. SLAB PULL (roughly 90% of the driving force) — cold, dense subducted lithosphere sinking under its own negative buoyancy, dragging the trailing plate. Oceanic lithosphere becomes denser than the underlying asthenosphere at about 30 Ma, which is why old, cold plates such as the Pacific move fastest.
2. RIDGE PUSH (a gravitational sliding force from the elevated ridge — properly, a body force from the thickening, cooling lithosphere).
3. BASAL DRAG from mantle convection, which can also resist motion.
The underlying energy is Earth's internal heat, about 47 TW, roughly half from radioactive decay of ²³⁸U, ²³⁵U, ²³²Th and ⁴⁰K, and half residual heat from accretion and core formation. Mantle convection cells transport this heat; the plates are the cold, rigid top thermal boundary layer of that convection, not passengers on it.

sections.heading: The three plate boundaries and what each builds
sections.body:
DIVERGENT — plates move apart; new lithosphere is created. Under oceans this makes MID-OCEAN RIDGES (the 65,000 km global ridge system). Decompression melting occurs because rising mantle crosses its solidus without gaining heat: pressure drops, melting point drops, melt forms. Rates: slow-spreading ridges such as the Mid-Atlantic move 2–5 cm/yr and have a deep axial rift valley; fast-spreading ridges such as the East Pacific Rise move 6–16 cm/yr and have a smooth axial high. Earthquakes are shallow (under 20 km) and small (rarely above M6). Volcanism is basaltic and effusive. On continents, divergence makes RIFT VALLEYS — the East African Rift, which will eventually become an ocean, as the Red Sea already has.
CONVERGENT — plates collide; lithosphere is destroyed or thickened. Three sub-types:
• Ocean-continent: the denser oceanic plate subducts, making a trench, then a continental volcanic arc 100–200 km inland (the Andes, the Cascades). Water driven off the descending slab at 80–120 km depth lowers the mantle wedge's melting point (FLUX MELTING), generating wet, silica-rich, gas-rich, explosive andesitic magma.
• Ocean-ocean: the older, colder plate subducts, making a trench and an ISLAND ARC (Japan, the Aleutians, the Marianas). The deepest point on Earth, Challenger Deep, is 10,935 m down in the Mariana Trench.
• Continent-continent: neither subducts because both are buoyant, so the crust thickens and shortens — the Himalaya, where India still drives north into Asia at about 5 cm/yr, having closed the Tethys Ocean over the last 50 Ma; Everest at 8849 m is still rising a few mm/yr.
TRANSFORM — plates slide past each other; lithosphere is neither created nor destroyed. Motion is horizontal (strike-slip). Most transforms offset mid-ocean ridge segments; the famous continental ones are the San Andreas (Pacific plate moving northwest relative to North America at about 3.5 cm/yr) and the North Anatolian Fault. Earthquakes are shallow and can be very large (M7–8), and because they are shallow they are disproportionately destructive. No volcanism.
HOTSPOTS are the exception to the rule: stationary (or slowly moving) mantle plumes not tied to a boundary. As the plate slides over the plume, it leaves an age-progressive chain of volcanoes. The Hawaiian-Emperor chain is the type example: Kilauea is active today, Kauai is about 5 Ma old, and the bend in the chain at about 47 Ma records a change in Pacific plate motion. Yellowstone is a continental hotspot; Iceland is a plume sitting on a ridge, which is why it is so volcanically productive.

sections.heading: Earthquakes: mechanics and measurement
sections.body:
MECHANISM — elastic rebound theory (Reid, 1910). Tectonic stress strains rock elastically along a locked fault; when the accumulated shear stress exceeds the frictional strength, the fault ruptures, the rock snaps back, and the stored elastic strain energy radiates as seismic waves. The FOCUS (hypocentre) is the point at depth where the rupture begins; the EPICENTRE is the point on the surface directly above it. Depths: shallow 0–70 km (about 75% of all quakes and most of the damage), intermediate 70–300 km, deep 300–700 km (only in subducting slabs; below 700 km rock is too ductile to fail brittlely).
WAVES, in arrival order: P (fastest, ~6 km/s in crust, a push-pull that arrives as a sharp bang), S (~3.5 km/s, side-to-side shear, stronger shaking), then SURFACE waves — Love waves (horizontal shearing) and Rayleigh waves (a rolling, elliptical motion). Surface waves are slowest but have the largest amplitude and do most of the damage to buildings.
LOCATING AN EPICENTRE — the S-minus-P method. The lag between the P and S arrivals grows with distance: d ≈ Δt × (v_p·v_s)/(v_p − v_s). With v_p = 6.0 km/s and v_s = 3.5 km/s the factor is (6.0 × 3.5)/(6.0 − 3.5) = 8.4 km per second of lag. WORKED EXAMPLE: a station records the S wave 20 s after the P wave → d ≈ 20 × 8.4 = 168 km. That gives a circle of radius 168 km around the station; three stations' circles intersect at one point — trilateration. This is exactly how epicentres were found before computers.
MAGNITUDE vs. INTENSITY — do not confuse them. MAGNITUDE is a single number measuring energy released at the source. The modern standard is MOMENT MAGNITUDE, M_w = (2/3)·log₁₀(M₀) − 10.7, with the seismic moment M₀ = µ·A·D in dyne·cm, where µ is the shear modulus of the rock (typically 3×10¹¹ dyne/cm²), A the rupture area (cm²) and D the average slip (cm). It is logarithmic: each whole step is 10× the ground-motion amplitude and about 31.6× the energy (because energy ∝ 10^1.5M). So M7 releases about 1000× the energy of M5, and the M9.5 Chile 1960 event released more energy than all other 20th-century quakes combined. INTENSITY (Modified Mercalli, I–XII) measures observed shaking and damage at a place, so one earthquake has many intensities, decreasing with distance and varying wildly with ground conditions.
SECONDARY HAZARDS: LIQUEFACTION, where saturated loose sand loses all strength as shaking raises pore water pressure until the effective stress σ' = σ − u falls to zero and buildings sink or float; landslides; fire from ruptured gas lines (which caused about 80% of the destruction in San Francisco 1906); and TSUNAMI. A tsunami's speed is v = √(g·d), with g = 9.81 m/s² and d the water depth in metres: over 4000 m of ocean, v = √(9.81 × 4000) ≈ 198 m/s ≈ 715 km/h — as fast as a jet. In deep water the wave may be under 1 m high with a wavelength of 200 km, undetectable to a ship; as depth shallows the speed drops, the energy compresses, and the wave height multiplies.

sections.heading: Volcanoes: why some ooze and some explode
sections.body:
The single most important variable is MAGMA VISCOSITY, which is controlled by silica content, temperature and dissolved gas. Silica tetrahedra polymerise into chains and networks; more SiO₂ means more polymerisation, higher viscosity, and gas that cannot escape. Higher temperature breaks those bonds and lowers viscosity.
• BASALTIC magma: 45–55% SiO₂, 1000–1200 °C, low viscosity (10²–10³ Pa·s), gas escapes freely → EFFUSIVE eruption, fluid lava flows moving up to 30 km/h (rarely; typically under walking pace), Hawaiian or Strombolian style. Builds SHIELD VOLCANOES — broad, gentle slopes of 2–10°. Mauna Loa is 120 km across and 9 km tall from its seafloor base, the largest single mountain on Earth by volume.
• ANDESITIC magma: 55–65% SiO₂, 800–1000 °C, intermediate viscosity → alternating explosive and effusive activity, Vulcanian/Peléan style. Builds STRATOVOLCANOES (composite cones) — steep 30–35° cones of interlayered lava and pyroclastics. Fuji, Rainier, Vesuvius, Mayon.
• RHYOLITIC magma: 65–75% SiO₂, 650–800 °C, extreme viscosity (10⁶–10¹² Pa·s), gas trapped at high pressure → catastrophically EXPLOSIVE, Plinian style. Builds lava domes and CALDERAS — collapse basins tens of kilometres across (Yellowstone, Toba, Campi Flegrei).
The eruption trigger is exsolution: dissolved H₂O and CO₂ come out of solution as magma rises and pressure drops (Henry's law — solubility is proportional to pressure). In fluid basalt the bubbles simply escape. In viscous rhyolite they cannot, so gas pressure builds until the magma fragments explosively, which is precisely the mechanism of a shaken carbonated drink.
VEI, the Volcanic Explosivity Index, is logarithmic in erupted tephra volume: VEI 0 under 10⁴ m³ (effusive), VEI 2 above 10⁶ m³, VEI 4 above 10⁹ m³ (Eyjafjallajökull 2010), VEI 5 above 10¹⁰ m³ (St. Helens 1980, Vesuvius 79 CE), VEI 6 above 10¹¹ m³ (Pinatubo 1991, Krakatoa 1883), VEI 7 above 10¹² m³ (Tambora 1815), VEI 8 above 10¹³ m³ (Toba ~74 ka, Yellowstone ~640 ka).
HAZARDS, ranked by lethality — and note that lava flows are near the bottom, because they are usually slow enough to walk away from:
1. PYROCLASTIC DENSITY CURRENTS — ground-hugging avalanches of gas and ash at 100–700 °C moving 100–700 km/h. Unsurvivable, unoutrunnable. These killed the population of Pompeii and Herculaneum and the 28,000 people of Saint-Pierre, Martinique in 1902.
2. LAHARS — volcanic mudflows of ash and water with the consistency of wet concrete, travelling 50–100 km/h and following valleys for tens of kilometres. Nevado del Ruiz, Colombia, 1985: a small VEI 3 eruption melted a summit glacier and the lahar buried the town of Armero, killing about 23,000 people 50 km from the volcano.
3. ASH FALL — collapses roofs at loads over about 100 kg/m² (roughly 10 cm of wet ash), destroys engines, contaminates water, and causes respiratory illness. It is abrasive, angular volcanic glass, not soft like wood ash.
4. VOLCANIC GASES — CO₂ is denser than air and pools invisibly in hollows; the 1986 Lake Nyos limnic eruption released a CO₂ cloud that asphyxiated about 1746 people. SO₂ forms sulphuric acid aerosols.
5. CLIMATE EFFECT — Tambora's 1815 SO₂ injection into the stratosphere caused the "Year Without a Summer" in 1816, cooling the Northern Hemisphere by roughly 0.4–0.7 °C and causing crop failure and famine; Pinatubo 1991 cooled global mean temperature about 0.5 °C for two years.

sections.heading: Practical survival: earthquake, tsunami and volcano
sections.body:
EARTHQUAKE — the evidence-based action is DROP, COVER, HOLD ON. Drop to hands and knees before the shaking drops you; take cover under a sturdy table (or, if none, against an interior wall away from windows, covering head and neck); hold on to the furniture and move with it. Do NOT run outside during shaking — most injuries come from falling debris at building exteriors, and doorways in modern buildings are no stronger than any other wall. Do not use lifts. If in bed, stay there and cover your head with a pillow, unless you are under a heavy light fitting. If outdoors, move to open ground away from buildings, power lines and walls. If driving, pull over clear of overpasses, bridges and wires, stay in the vehicle, set the handbrake. AFTER: expect aftershocks (the largest aftershock is typically about 1.2 magnitude units below the mainshock, and aftershock frequency decays as roughly 1/t — Omori's law); check for gas smells and shut off the supply only if you smell or hear a leak; wear sturdy shoes for broken glass; expect utilities to be out for days; text rather than call to keep networks clear. PREPARE: bolt tall furniture and water heaters to studs, keep 4 litres of water per person per day for 7 days, keep shoes and a torch by the bed.
TSUNAMI — the natural warning signs mean you evacuate immediately without waiting for an official alert. If you feel an earthquake strong enough that standing is difficult, or one lasting more than about 20 seconds, near the coast; or if the sea suddenly withdraws exposing the seafloor; or if you hear a loud roar from the sea — GO. Move immediately on foot (roads jam) to at least 30 m above sea level or 3 km inland, whichever comes first, and stay there. The first wave is often not the largest; the sequence can continue for 8–12 hours with waves 10–60 minutes apart. Never go down to look. A 30 cm flow can knock an adult over and a 1 m flow moves cars.
VOLCANO — obey exclusion zones absolutely; they are drawn around the pyroclastic-flow and lahar reach, not the lava. Never enter a valley draining a snow-capped or erupting volcano, and if you feel shaking or hear a roar in such a valley, climb sideways to high ground at once — 20–30 m of vertical elevation out of the channel is enough to survive most lahars. For ash fall: stay indoors, close windows and vents, wear an N95/P2 respirator or at minimum a damp cloth, wear goggles rather than contact lenses (ash under a lens abrades the cornea), sweep ash off roofs before it exceeds about 10 cm (wet ash weighs roughly twice dry ash, near 1000 kg/m³), and do not drive — ash makes roads slick and destroys engines through the air intake. Do not shelter in a basement or low hollow if there is any chance of CO₂ accumulation.
COMMON MISTAKES: believing the "triangle of life" myth (discredited — do not lie beside furniture); believing small quakes "relieve pressure" (it takes about 32,000 M4 events to release the energy of one M7); assuming animals give reliable warning; assuming a distant volcano is safe (lahars and ash reach far beyond the visible mountain); and assuming a river valley beside a coast is safe from a tsunami — tsunamis run far up river channels.

sections.heading: Paleomagnetism and the Seafloor Stripes That Proved It All
sections.body: Plate tectonics went from a fringe idea (Alfred Wegener's continental drift, proposed in 1912 and dismissed for decades for lacking a mechanism) to established science largely because of rock magnetism. As basaltic lava cools through its Curie point (around 580°C for magnetite), its magnetic minerals lock into alignment with Earth's field at that moment, like a compass needle frozen mid-swing — remanent magnetism. Earth's field has flipped polarity hundreds of times over geologic history, at irregular intervals averaging a few hundred thousand years, and each reversal is recorded in freshly formed rock. In the early 1960s, magnetometer surveys towed behind ships crossing mid-ocean ridges revealed bands of alternating normal and reversed polarity running parallel to the ridge crest, symmetric on both sides like a barcode mirrored left and right. Geologists Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews (and independently Lawrence Morley) realized in 1963 this was exactly what seafloor spreading would produce: new crust wells up at the ridge axis, splits in two, and rafts away in both directions at a steady rate, each half recording the same sequence of reversals as it cools. Match stripe width to the independently known ages of reversals and you get a precise spreading rate — the Atlantic ridge spreads roughly 2–5 cm per year, about the rate fingernails grow, while the East Pacific Rise spreads up to 15 cm per year. This single dataset did more than any other to convert plate tectonics from hypothesis to measured fact, giving geologists an actual clock and ruler for something previously inferred only from the jigsaw-fit of coastlines.

sections.heading: Hotspots and Mantle Plumes: Volcanoes That Don't Follow the Boundary Rule
sections.body: Almost all volcanism happens at plate boundaries — but the Hawaiian Islands sit in the dead center of the Pacific Plate, thousands of kilometers from the nearest margin, and are among the most active volcanoes on Earth. The explanation, proposed by J. Tuzo Wilson in 1963, is a hotspot: a plume of unusually hot rock rising from deep in the mantle that stays essentially fixed while the plate above it drifts overhead. The plate does the moving, so a hotspot burns a chain of volcanoes into the seafloor like a blowtorch held under paper being dragged across it — each island progressively older and more eroded the farther it sits from the currently active volcano. The Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain is the textbook case: Kīlauea sits directly over the hotspot today; the chain continues as submerged seamounts stretching over 5,800 km to the Aleutian Trench, with ages increasing systematically to over 80 million years. A striking ~60-degree bend around 47 million years ago is long debated as evidence the Pacific Plate changed direction, a puzzle that sharpens how geologists think about whether 'fixed' hotspots really are fixed. Not every hotspot is oceanic: Yellowstone sits atop a continental hotspot, and the Snake River Plain shows a matching age-progressive trail of ancient calderas leading back toward it — the same mechanism erupting through continental crust, producing far more violent, silica-rich eruptions as a result.

sections.heading: Historical Earthquakes and Eruptions That Rewrote Hazard Science
sections.body: Several individual disasters didn't just cause damage — they directly changed how the science is done. The 1906 San Francisco earthquake led geologist Henry Fielding Reid to survey ground displacement along the San Andreas Fault and notice offset greatest right at the fault, tapering with distance — from this he formulated elastic rebound theory in 1910, still the core model: rock deforms elastically for decades as tectonic stress slowly builds, then snaps back past its original position when it breaks, releasing seismic waves. The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile, magnitude 9.5, remains the largest ever instrumentally recorded and helped establish the moment magnitude scale as necessary — the older Richter scale saturates and systematically underestimates events this size. The 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens produced a lateral blast after a huge chunk of the volcano's bulging north flank slid away in the largest landslide in recorded history, exposing the pressurized magma system to a near-instant pressure drop; volcanologists had not planned hazard zones for a sideways blast, and the event rewrote volcanic hazard mapping to include lateral blast zones, not just downslope pyroclastic-flow and lahar paths. The 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo injected roughly 20 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, forming a global sulfate haze that measurably cooled average global temperatures by about 0.5°C for over a year — direct, measured proof large eruptions can brake global climate, a mechanism now built into climate models.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: You don't need a seismic network to start observing plate tectonics in action — a surprising amount is within reach with basic gear plus attention to public data.
ingredients: A topographic or geologic map of your region (many national geological surveys publish these freely) to locate nearby faults, volcanic fields, or uplifted terrain
A compass and clinometer, or a smartphone compass/clinometer app, for measuring strike and dip of exposed rock near a fault
A basic rock hammer and hand lens for examining volcanic or fault-zone rock samples up close
Sturdy closed-toe boots, work gloves, and safety glasses for any visit to a fault scarp, quarry, or volcanic outcrop
A dust mask or respirator rated for fine particulates if visiting any site with volcanic ash — ash is sharp-edged glass shards microscopically and genuinely damaging to lungs with prolonged exposure
Simple building materials (a wooden board, string, a heavy weight such as a fishing sinker or metal washer, a pen, and a roll of paper) to build a basic pendulum seismometer
Access to a public earthquake catalog (most national geological surveys publish free, real-time earthquake location and magnitude data) for plotting recent seismicity against a plate boundary map

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Build a Simple Pendulum Seismometer and Record Real Ground Motion
sections.body: A working seismometer that can register footsteps, a slammed door, or a passing truck can be built on a kitchen table in under an hour — the same basic physics as professional instruments, just far less sensitive.
steps: Fix a sturdy board or heavy frame to a solid surface (a table pressed against a wall, or a shelf bolted to a stud) so it won't wobble independently of the ground.
Hang a weight (200–500 g, such as a padlock or a bag of washers) from a length of string about 30–40 cm long, tied to the fixed frame, forming a simple pendulum.
Tape a pen or fine marker to the bottom of the hanging weight, pointing straight down, with the tip just barely touching a horizontal surface below.

Place a long strip of paper on that surface, positioned so the pen tip rests near one end, and set up a way to draw the paper under the pen over several minutes — even manually, at a slow steady rate — as your recording drum.
Let the pendulum settle to a full stop before starting a recording so your baseline is a straight line.

Generate a test disturbance — have someone jump near the table, or gently tap the frame — and watch the pen trace deviate from the straight line; note the amplitude and how long the oscillation takes to die out.

Compare traces from different disturbances (a light tap vs. a heavy footstep vs. a nearby door slam) and record which produces the largest amplitude — this mirrors how a real seismogram distinguishes a small local event from a larger, more distant one.

Look up a recent moderate earthquake in a public earthquake catalog and note its magnitude and distance from a seismic station, then consider why your tabletop pendulum, unlike a real seismometer, is far too damped and insensitive to register any actual earthquake — real instruments use a near-frictionless suspended mass and electromagnetic sensors because distant ground motion is measured in micrometers.

guides.title: The Water Cycle & Hydrology
guides.summary: Where Earth's water is, the physics that moves it, how rivers and groundwater actually work, how to read a catchment, and how to find, judge and treat water in the field.

sections.heading: The global water budget: where the water actually is
sections.body:
Earth holds about 1.386 × 10⁹ km³ (1.386 billion cubic kilometres) of water. Its distribution is startlingly lopsided:
• Oceans (saline): 1,338,000,000 km³ — 96.5%
• Ice caps, glaciers and permanent snow: 24,064,000 km³ — 1.74%
• Groundwater: 23,400,000 km³ — 1.69% (of which only about 10,530,000 km³, 0.76% of the total, is fresh)
• Ground ice and permafrost: 300,000 km³ — 0.022%
• Lakes: 176,400 km³ — 0.013% (91,000 km³ fresh)
• Soil moisture: 16,500 km³ — 0.001%
• Atmosphere: 12,900 km³ — 0.001%
• Swamps and marshes: 11,470 km³
• Rivers: 2,120 km³ — 0.0002%
• Biological water (in living things): 1,120 km³
So fresh water is only about 2.5% of the total, and roughly 69% of THAT is locked in ice, 30% is groundwater, and well under 1% is in the accessible surface water that supports nearly all terrestrial life. All the world's rivers together hold about 2100 km³ — less than one part in 650,000 of Earth's water — yet they carry the bulk of the flux.
GLOBAL FLUXES per year: about 505,000 km³ evaporates (434,000 from the ocean, 71,000 from land), and the same falls as precipitation (398,000 over the ocean, 107,000 over land). The land therefore receives 36,000 km³ more than it evaporates, and exactly that surplus returns to the sea as river discharge and groundwater flow. This is the closure condition of the water cycle: over the long term, global evaporation equals global precipitation.
RESIDENCE TIME, τ = V / Q, where V is the stored volume and Q the flux through the reservoir, tells you how long a water molecule stays put: atmosphere about 9 days (which is why weather is predictable only for about a week), rivers 2–6 months, soil moisture 1–2 months, lakes 50–100 years, shallow groundwater 100–200 years, deep groundwater up to 10,000 years, oceans about 3200 years, Antarctic ice up to 800,000 years. That the atmosphere holds only 12,900 km³ but cycles 505,000 km³ per year means the entire atmospheric water content turns over about 39 times a year.

sections.heading: The physics: why water moves at all
sections.body:
Water is driven around the planet by solar energy and gravity, and its unusual molecular properties do the rest. Water's polarity and hydrogen bonding give it: a specific heat capacity of 4184 J/(kg·K) — the highest of any common liquid, which moderates climate; a latent heat of vaporisation of 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg at 100 °C (about 2.45 × 10⁶ J/kg at 20 °C) — evaporating 1 kg of water absorbs as much energy as heating that kilogram by 540 °C would; a latent heat of fusion of 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg; and a maximum density at 4 °C, so ice floats and lakes freeze from the top down, protecting aquatic life.
EVAPORATION requires energy and a vapour-pressure deficit. Saturation vapour pressure rises roughly exponentially with temperature — the Clausius-Clapeyron relation gives about 7% more water vapour capacity per 1 °C of warming. A workable approximation is e_s(T) = 0.6108 · exp(17.27·T / (T + 237.3)), with e_s in kilopascals and T in °C. At 20 °C, e_s ≈ 2.34 kPa; at 30 °C, e_s ≈ 4.24 kPa — nearly double. RELATIVE HUMIDITY, RH = (e / e_s) × 100%, where e is the actual vapour pressure. The DEW POINT is the temperature at which the air becomes saturated (e = e_s); condensation begins there, and it is the number that actually tells you how muggy the air is.
EVAPOTRANSPIRATION (ET) is evaporation from surfaces plus transpiration through plant stomata; over vegetated land, transpiration usually dominates. A single large oak can transpire 150–400 litres per day; a hectare of maize about 40,000 litres per day at peak growth.
CONDENSATION AND PRECIPITATION: air rises, expands against lower pressure, and cools without exchanging heat (adiabatically). The dry adiabatic lapse rate is 9.8 °C per km of ascent; once saturated, latent heat release slows this to a saturated adiabatic lapse rate of about 4–7 °C/km. When the parcel cools to its dew point, water condenses onto cloud condensation nuclei (dust, salt, sulphates, pollen — 0.2–2 µm). Cloud droplets are only about 20 µm across and fall too slowly to reach the ground; they must grow to about 500–1000 µm by collision-coalescence, or via the Bergeron process in which ice crystals grow at the expense of supercooled droplets because saturation vapour pressure over ice is lower than over water. Four lifting mechanisms produce rain: CONVECTIVE (surface heating — thunderstorms), OROGRAPHIC (air forced over mountains, giving a wet windward side and a dry RAIN SHADOW leeward — the Atacama, Death Valley and the Tibetan Plateau all exist for this reason), FRONTAL (warm air riding over cold), and CONVERGENT (air piling into a low-pressure zone).

sections.heading: Catchments, runoff and the water balance
sections.body:
A CATCHMENT (watershed, drainage basin) is the entire area of land whose precipitation drains to one common outlet. Catchments are separated by DIVIDES — the ridge lines. Every point on Earth is in exactly one catchment at every scale, nested like a tree. Stream ORDER (Strahler) formalises the tree: a headwater stream with no tributaries is order 1; two order-1 streams join to make an order 2; two order-2s make an order 3; an order-1 joining an order-3 leaves it order 3. The Amazon is order 12. Each order up, the number of streams falls by roughly a factor of 3–5 and the average length rises by a similar factor.
The WATER BALANCE EQUATION is the master accounting identity for any catchment over any period:
P = Q + ET + ΔS
where P = precipitation (mm), Q = runoff/streamflow leaving the basin (mm), ET = evapotranspiration (mm) and ΔS = change in storage (soil moisture + groundwater + snowpack + surface water, mm). All terms are usually expressed as a depth of water over the whole catchment area. Over a long enough period (many years) ΔS ≈ 0, so P ≈ Q + ET.
WORKED EXAMPLE. A catchment of 250 km² receives 900 mm/yr of precipitation. Measured streamflow at the outlet averages 4.0 m³/s. Convert flow to a depth: annual volume = 4.0 m³/s × 31,557,600 s = 1.262 × 10⁸ m³. Divided by the area, 250 km² = 2.5 × 10⁸ m², gives 0.505 m = 505 mm. So Q = 505 mm. Assuming ΔS ≈ 0, ET = P − Q = 900 − 505 = 395 mm/yr. The RUNOFF COEFFICIENT is Q/P = 505/900 = 0.56, meaning 56% of rainfall leaves as streamflow — typical of a temperate, moderately vegetated basin. A forested tropical basin might be 0.2; a paved urban basin 0.8–0.95.
When rain falls it partitions: INTERCEPTION (caught on leaves, 10–40% of small rainfalls in forest, mostly re-evaporated), INFILTRATION into soil, and OVERLAND FLOW when rainfall intensity exceeds infiltration capacity (Hortonian) or when the soil saturates from below (saturation-excess). Infiltration capacity is high at the start of a storm and decays toward the soil's saturated hydraulic conductivity — sand 20–100 mm/hr, silt loam 5–20 mm/hr, clay 0.1–1 mm/hr. This is why the same 30 mm/hr downpour runs straight off clay and vanishes into sand.
The STORM HYDROGRAPH plots discharge against time: a rising limb, a peak, then a long recession limb, with LAG TIME between the rainfall centroid and the peak. Urbanisation, deforestation, steep slopes, thin soils and antecedent wetness all shorten lag time and raise the peak — this is precisely the mechanism of flash flooding. BASE FLOW, the discharge sustained between storms, is groundwater seeping into the channel; a river that keeps flowing in drought is being fed by its aquifer.

sections.heading: Rivers: how channels do their work
sections.body:
DISCHARGE is the fundamental measurement: Q = A × v, where Q is discharge in m³/s (cumecs), A the cross-sectional area of flow in m², and v the mean velocity in m/s. To measure it in the field: stretch a tape across the channel, divide the width into 10–20 segments, at each segment measure depth and measure velocity at 0.6 of the depth from the surface (that single point closely approximates the depth-averaged velocity), then sum A_i × v_i over all segments. A rough float method: time a floating object over a measured 10 m reach, take the mean of at least 3 trials, and multiply the surface velocity by 0.85 to estimate the mean.
MANNING'S EQUATION predicts velocity from channel geometry:
v = (1/n) · R^(2/3) · S^(1/2)
where v is mean velocity (m/s), n is Manning's roughness coefficient (dimensionless: 0.010 for smooth concrete, 0.030 for a clean natural earth channel, 0.040 for a gravel-bed stream with weeds, 0.070–0.15 for a heavily vegetated floodplain), R is the hydraulic radius = A/P with P the wetted perimeter (m), and S is the energy slope (m/m, approximated by the water-surface slope). WORKED EXAMPLE: a channel 8 m wide and 1.2 m deep has A = 9.6 m², wetted perimeter P = 8 + 2(1.2) = 10.4 m, so R = 0.923 m. With a gravel bed (n = 0.040) and a slope of 0.002, v = (1/0.040) × 0.923^0.667 × 0.002^0.5 = 25 × 0.948 × 0.0447 = 1.06 m/s. Discharge Q = 9.6 × 1.06 ≈ 10.2 m³/s.
SEDIMENT AND ENERGY. A river transports material as dissolved load, suspended load (which makes it look brown and is usually the largest fraction by mass), and bed load (rolling, sliding and saltating grains). The HJULSTRÖM CURVE captures a counterintuitive fact: the velocity needed to ERODE a particle is not a simple function of grain size. Sand around 0.2–0.5 mm is entrained at the lowest velocity, about 20–30 cm/s. Coarser gravel needs more velocity because it is heavier; but fine clay ALSO needs more velocity (up to 100 cm/s) because electrostatic cohesion binds the platelets. Once moving, however, clay stays in suspension almost indefinitely — it only settles below about 0.1 cm/s. This is why muddy water clears so slowly, and why a dredged clay bank resists re-erosion.
CHANNEL FORMS. Steep headwaters are straight and boulder-choked with a V-shaped valley, high gradient, and erosion dominant. Middle reaches MEANDER: flow spirals helically, eroding the outside of a bend (the cut bank, deep, fast) and depositing on the inside (the point bar, shallow, slow). Meander wavelength is empirically about 10–14 times the channel width. Necks eventually cut through, abandoning an OXBOW LAKE. Lower reaches are low-gradient, deposit-dominated, and build floodplains, levees and finally a DELTA where the current dies at the sea. The GRADED PROFILE — steep at the head, concave, near-flat at the mouth — is a river's equilibrium form, adjusting toward the minimum work needed to transport its sediment load.
FLOODS are described by RECURRENCE INTERVAL: T = (n + 1)/m, where n is the number of years of record and m is the rank of the flood by size. A "100-year flood" has a 1% chance of being exceeded in any given year — it is a probability, not a schedule, and two can occur in consecutive years. The probability of at least one T-year flood in N years is 1 − (1 − 1/T)^N; over a 30-year mortgage, the chance of at least one 100-year flood is 1 − 0.99³⁰ = 26%.

sections.heading: Groundwater: the invisible reservoir
sections.body:
Rain that infiltrates percolates down through the UNSATURATED (vadose) zone, where pores hold both air and water, to the WATER TABLE — the surface below which every pore is full. Below that is the SATURATED zone. The water table is not flat; it is a subdued replica of the topography, higher under hills and intersecting the surface at springs, lakes and perennial streams.
TWO PROPERTIES govern everything. POROSITY (n) is the percentage of a rock's volume that is void space — gravel 25–40%, sand 25–50%, clay 40–70%, fractured basalt 5–50%, unfractured granite under 1%. PERMEABILITY (hydraulic conductivity, K, in m/day) is the ability to TRANSMIT water, which depends on whether the pores connect and how large they are. Clay has enormous porosity but almost no permeability, because its pores are microscopic and water is held by surface tension — this is the crucial distinction and the most common misunderstanding in hydrogeology. Typical K: gravel 100–1000 m/day, coarse sand 10–100, fine sand 1–10, silt 0.001–0.1, clay 10⁻⁶–10⁻³.
DARCY'S LAW governs groundwater flow:
Q = −K · A · (dh/dl)
where Q is volumetric flow (m³/day), K hydraulic conductivity (m/day), A cross-sectional area (m²), and dh/dl the hydraulic gradient (the drop in head per unit distance, dimensionless). The negative sign means flow goes from high head to low head. WORKED EXAMPLE: an aquifer of coarse sand (K = 30 m/day) is 10 m thick and 200 m wide (A = 2000 m²), and the water table falls 4 m over 800 m of distance (gradient = 0.005). Q = 30 × 2000 × 0.005 = 300 m³/day. The actual water velocity is much slower than this bulk flux suggests: seepage velocity v = K·(dh/dl)/n = 30 × 0.005 / 0.30 = 0.5 m/day. Groundwater typically moves centimetres to a few metres per day — a contaminant plume may take decades to reach a well, and an aquifer polluted today may not be recognised as polluted for a generation.
AQUIFER TYPES: an UNCONFINED aquifer has the water table as its upper surface and is recharged directly from above (and is therefore vulnerable to surface pollution). A CONFINED aquifer is sandwiched between AQUITARDS (low-permeability layers) and is under pressure; drilling into one produces an ARTESIAN well, where water rises above the top of the aquifer, and sometimes flows at the surface without pumping. A PERCHED aquifer sits on a local impermeable lens above the regional water table.
Pumping creates a CONE OF DEPRESSION around a well; over-pumping causes wells to go dry, land SUBSIDENCE (California's San Joaquin Valley has sunk over 8.5 m in places), and SALTWATER INTRUSION at coasts. The Ghyben-Herzberg relation quantifies the last: because fresh water (1000 kg/m³) floats on salt water (1025 kg/m³), z = 40h, meaning for every 1 m the water table sits above sea level, the fresh-water lens extends about 40 m below sea level. Drop the water table 1 m by pumping and the salt interface rises 40 m — which is why small-island and coastal aquifers fail so abruptly.

sections.heading: Finding water in the field: reading the landscape
sections.body:
The hydrological principles above translate directly into where to look when you need water and have no map.
1. FOLLOW GRAVITY AND GREEN. Water collects in the lowest point of any drainage. Trace valleys and gullies downhill; walk toward converging contours. Vegetation is the best indicator: a distinct line or clump of greener, denser, broadleaf growth in dry country marks shallow water. Willows, cottonwoods, sycamores, cattails, reeds, sedges and rushes are phreatophytes — their roots reach the water table, so they mark it. A band of them across a dry hillside marks a seep line.
2. READ THE GEOLOGY. Springs emerge where a permeable layer sits on an impermeable one and the contact is exposed — look along the base of a sandstone or limestone cliff where it meets shale, along fault traces, and at the foot of talus slopes. In limestone country, look for resurgences at the base of hills. At the toe of any large debris or scree slope, water that sank into the coarse material often reappears.
3. DIG, DON'T DESPAIR. In a dry sandy or gravelly streambed, dig on the OUTSIDE of the last bend (the deepest scour, the cut bank), on the downstream side of any obstruction, or at the lowest point. Dig a hole 30–60 cm across and go down 30–100 cm; let it fill and settle for 30+ minutes so silt drops out. This is a seepage well, and it also filters the water through sand, though it does NOT make it microbiologically safe.
4. COASTS AND DUNES. Fresh rainwater floats as a thin lens on salt water. Dig behind the first dune line, above the high-tide mark, only until water appears — dig deeper and you break into salt. Skim the top of the water.
5. COLLECT DIRECTLY. Rainfall from a tarp or poncho funnel is the cleanest source available and needs no treatment if the collecting surface is clean. Dew: drag an absorbent cloth over grass before dawn and wring it out; a person can gather 0.5–1 litre per hour on a heavy dew. Snow and ice: always melt before drinking — eating snow costs 334 kJ per kg of body heat and accelerates hypothermia. Melt old, compacted snow or ice, which yields far more water per volume than fresh powder.
6. TRANSPIRATION BAG. Tie a clear plastic bag over a leafy, non-toxic branch in sun with a weighted low corner; transpired vapour condenses and collects. Yield is modest — 50–250 mL per bag per day — and you must verify the plant is not toxic (avoid oleander, yew, poison ivy/oak/sumac and any milky-sapped plant). A SOLAR STILL dug in soil is usually not worth the calories: typical yield is under 500 mL/day for hours of digging, less than the sweat spent.
WHAT TO AVOID: stagnant water with no outlet, no insects and no green plants around it; water with a chemical or petroleum sheen (a bacterial iron sheen breaks into plates when poked, an oil sheen swirls back together); water downstream of mines, tailings, farms, feedlots or industry; and alkali flats where salt crusts show at the edges. Never drink seawater or urine — both raise your osmotic load and dehydrate you faster.

sections.heading: Making water safe: treatment methods with real numbers
sections.body:
Water carries three hazard classes and no single field method removes all three. PATHOGENS: protozoan cysts (Giardia 8–12 µm, Cryptosporidium 4–6 µm — the latter highly chlorine-resistant), bacteria (E. coli, Salmonella, Vibrio cholerae, 0.2–5 µm), and viruses (hepatitis A, rotavirus, norovirus, 0.02–0.1 µm). CHEMICALS: arsenic, nitrate, fluoride, lead, pesticides, industrial solvents. TURBIDITY: suspended sediment, which is not itself dangerous but shields pathogens from disinfection and consumes chemical disinfectant.
STEP 1 — CLARIFY FIRST, ALWAYS. Every disinfection method works far better on clear water. Let sediment settle for several hours; decant the clear top. Then filter through tightly woven cloth folded 4–8 times, or through a simple gravity column: a container with a small hole, packed bottom-up with cloth, then 10 cm of clean coarse gravel, 10 cm of coarse sand, 15–20 cm of fine sand, and optionally 5 cm of crushed charcoal from a hardwood fire (charcoal adsorbs some organics, tastes and odours — it does NOT disinfect and it exhausts within days). Discard the first litre through a new column.
STEP 2 — DISINFECT. Choose by hazard:
• BOILING — the gold standard, kills everything biological. Bring to a rolling boil and hold 1 minute at sea level; hold 3 minutes above 2000 m (water boils at about 93 °C at 2000 m and 80 °C at 6000 m, but pasteurisation still occurs at 70 °C given time). Boiling does NOT remove chemicals, salts or heavy metals — it concentrates them.
• CHLORINE (unscented household bleach, sodium hypochlorite). For 5–6% bleach: 2 drops per litre of clear water, 4 drops per litre if cold or cloudy. For 8.25% bleach: 2 drops per litre. Stir, wait 30 minutes (60 minutes if the water is below 10 °C or cloudy). The water should have a faint chlorine smell; if not, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes. Kills bacteria and viruses reliably; kills Giardia given time; does NOT reliably kill Cryptosporidium. Use only plain bleach — no scent, no detergent, no thickener — and note bleach loses roughly half its strength per year.
• IODINE (2% tincture): 5 drops per litre clear, 10 drops per litre cloudy, wait 30 minutes (longer when cold). Not for pregnant women, people with thyroid disorders, or continuous use beyond a few weeks. Ineffective against Cryptosporidium.
• SODIS (solar disinfection) — fill a clear PET plastic bottle (max 2 L, max 10 cm diameter) with clear water, lay it on its side on a reflective or dark surface, and expose to full sun for 6 hours (or 2 consecutive days if overcast). UV-A plus heat inactivates bacteria, viruses and protozoa. It requires genuinely clear water (you must be able to read text through the filled bottle) and does not work in glass, which blocks UV-A.
• FILTERS — a filter rated at 1 µm absolute removes protozoa and most bacteria but NOT viruses; a 0.2 µm filter removes bacteria too. Only a purifier rated to 0.02 µm or a chemical/UV step handles viruses. In a wilderness setting where viral contamination is unlikely, a good filter alone is usually sufficient; downstream of human habitation, always add a chemical or boiling step.
• DISTILLATION is the only field method that removes salt, heavy metals and most chemicals — condense steam on a cool surface and collect it. It is slow and fuel-expensive but it is the answer for seawater or chemically contaminated sources.
SAFETY AND COMMON MISTAKES. Do not assume clear, cold, fast-moving mountain water is safe — Giardia is common in pristine-looking streams. Do not rely on charcoal or a cloth filter as disinfection. Never mix bleach with ammonia or acids. Do not over-chlorinate hoping for extra safety. Store treated water in a clean, covered container and do not re-contaminate it with dirty hands or a dirty scoop. Rehydrating: an adult at rest in a temperate climate needs about 2–3 litres a day, rising to 4–6+ litres with heat and exertion; dark, scanty urine is the practical warning sign. If severe diarrhoea occurs after drinking suspect water, oral rehydration matters more than the underlying infection in the short term — the WHO oral rehydration formula is roughly 6 level teaspoons of sugar plus half a level teaspoon of salt in 1 litre of clean water. This is general education, not medical advice; seek professional medical care for persistent illness, bloody stools, high fever or signs of severe dehydration.

sections.heading: Stream Discharge and the Hydrograph: Reading a River's Pulse
sections.body: The single most useful number in hydrology is discharge — the volume of water passing a point per unit time, Q, in cubic meters per second. It's Q = A × V, cross-sectional area times average velocity, but both are fiddly to measure honestly, because velocity varies with depth (fastest just below the surface, slowest near the bed and banks) and area changes with stage. Hydrologists measure velocity at multiple verticals across the channel, typically at 0.6 of the depth from the surface (a good approximation of the vertically averaged velocity), then sum the discharge contribution from each subsection — the mid-section method. Plotted over time, discharge traces a hydrograph: a rising limb as runoff reaches the channel, a peak, then a longer falling limb called the recession. The shape is diagnostic. A small, paved urban catchment produces a 'flashy' hydrograph — a short lag time and a high, sharp peak, because impervious surfaces shed water almost instantly. A large, forested or wetland-rich catchment produces a 'damped' hydrograph — a long lag time and a lower, broader peak, because soil, vegetation, and groundwater storage delay and smooth the water's path to the channel. The discharge that persists even during dry weather — groundwater slowly draining into the channel — is baseflow, and the ratio of stormflow to baseflow is one of the clearest fingerprints of how much a landscape has been paved, farmed, or otherwise altered, which is exactly why urbanization is one of the most direct, measurable causes of increased downstream flooding, independent of any change in rainfall itself.

sections.heading: Water Quality Beyond Potability: Dissolved Oxygen and Eutrophication
sections.body: Making water safe to drink is a different question from whether water is healthy for the ecosystem living in it, and the two use almost entirely different numbers. The key ecological metric is dissolved oxygen (DO), in milligrams per liter; most fish need at least 4–5 mg/L, and levels below about 2 mg/L constitute hypoxia — a 'dead zone' where most aquatic life cannot survive. Cold water holds more dissolved oxygen than warm water, which is why thermal pollution can suppress DO even without adding a pollutant directly. The more dramatic mechanism is eutrophication: excess nitrogen and phosphorus from agricultural runoff, sewage, or detergents fuel explosive algae growth. When that algae dies, bacteria decomposing it consume oxygen faster than it can be replenished — quantified as biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), how much oxygen a water sample's own microbial community consumes over five days in the dark. High-BOD water warns of an oxygen crash to come. The textbook large-scale case is the Gulf of Mexico dead zone, forming most summers where the Mississippi River dumps a nitrogen- and phosphorus-rich plume into the Gulf; the resulting bloom and decomposition regularly creates a hypoxic zone of several thousand square miles. Turbidity (cloudiness from suspended sediment, measured in NTU or estimated with a Secchi disk lowered until it disappears from sight) compounds the problem by blocking sunlight from reaching submerged plants, themselves a major oxygen source for the water column.

sections.heading: Floods, Droughts, and the Return-Period Statistics Behind the Headlines
sections.body: When a report calls something a '100-year flood,' it states a probability, not a promise of spacing — a confusion behind some of the most consequential misunderstandings in applied hydrology. A flood's return period T is estimated from a discharge record using a plotting-position formula, commonly Weibull's T = (n + 1) / m, where n is years of record and m is the rank of a year's peak discharge sorted largest to smallest. A '100-year flood' is the discharge level with an estimated 1-in-100 chance of being equaled or exceeded in any given year — so a location can suffer two in consecutive years (rare but not a contradiction, like flipping heads twice running), and over a 30-year mortgage the cumulative probability of at least one is 1 − (0.99)^30 ≈ 26%, more than one in four. Drought is harder to define crisply because it's a sustained deficit, not a threshold crossing, so hydrologists use indices like the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), comparing accumulated precipitation over a window (commonly 3, 6, or 12 months) against the long-term historical distribution and expressing the deficit in standard deviations — an SPI of −2.0 means precipitation was roughly in the driest 2–3% of the historical record for that season. Both statistics share a caveat: they're only as good as the record they're built on, and a genuinely changing climate can make return-period estimates from 20th-century data underestimate 21st-century risk, a gap that catches infrastructure planners off guard more often than any single storm does.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: Real stream and rainfall measurements don't require a hydrology lab — a rain gauge and a stopwatch will get you genuine, useful numbers.
ingredients: A simple rain gauge (a clear straight-sided cylinder with graduated markings, or a purpose-built plastic gauge) mounted in an open spot away from overhanging trees or eaves — a garden center or hardware store
A stopwatch or any phone timer, for stream velocity timing
A tape measure (at least 10–15 m) for measuring channel width and depth at multiple points
A wading rod or a long straight stick marked with depth increments, for measuring depth safely without stepping into deep or fast water
A floating object of consistent buoyancy (an orange, a tennis ball, or a purpose-bought hydrology float) for surface-velocity timing
A secchi disk (a black-and-white weighted disk on a marked cord) or a simple turbidity tube, for water clarity — an aquarium/pond-supply or science-education shop
pH test strips or a digital pH meter, and if available a basic freshwater aquarium dissolved-oxygen or nitrate test kit (sold for fish-keeping and perfectly usable for field water quality)
A topographic map (paper or a mapping app with contour lines) for sketching your catchment boundary
A notebook and pencil for logging measurements — pencil is preferred over pen because it still writes when wet

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Measure Your Local Stream's Discharge and a Week of Rainfall
sections.body: This is the exact float method hydrologists used for a century before electronic flow meters became common, and it's still accurate enough for genuine field science.
steps: Choose a straight, uniform stretch of stream at least 10 meters long with no major obstructions, and mark the start and end points on both banks.

Measure the width of the channel at three cross-sections along the stretch, and at each measure depth at several evenly spaced points with your wading rod, always facing upstream and never wading into water above knee height or with visibly fast current.
Calculate the average cross-sectional area at each section by approximating each strip between depth measurements as a small rectangle or trapezoid and summing them.
Drop your floating object at the upstream mark and time how long it takes to reach the downstream mark; repeat three times and average the results for a surface velocity.
Multiply that surface velocity by 0.85 (a standard correction, since surface water moves faster than the depth-averaged velocity due to bed friction) to estimate mean velocity.
