Calculate discharge as Q = average cross-sectional area × corrected mean velocity, in cubic meters or feet per second.
Set up your rain gauge in an open location and record accumulated rainfall depth at the same time each day for one full week, resetting to zero after each reading.

At week's end, compare the timing of any rainfall against a change in the stream's discharge (repeat the discharge measurement after a rain event) — you should see a lag between rain and rise in flow, a direct measurement of your catchment's response time.

guides.title: Soil — How It Forms and Feeds Us
guides.summary: What soil actually is, the five factors and four processes that make it, how to read a soil profile and test texture by hand, the chemistry of pH and nutrients, and how to build and protect fertile ground.

sections.heading: What soil is: definition and composition
sections.body:
SOIL is the unconsolidated mineral and organic material at Earth's surface that has been altered in place by climate and organisms, and that serves as a medium for plant growth. It is not "dirt" (displaced soil) and it is not merely weathered rock (that is REGOLITH, the loose material from which soil develops). The distinguishing feature of soil is HORIZONATION — the development of distinct, roughly horizontal layers.
An ideal loam soil by VOLUME is about:
• 45% mineral matter (sand, silt, clay derived from rock)
• 25% water (in pores)
• 25% air (in pores)
• 5% organic matter (of which roughly 80% humus, 10% roots, 10% living organisms)
Note that half the volume is PORE SPACE, and that the water and air fractions trade against each other — a saturated soil has no air, and roots of most crops suffocate within 24–72 hours of waterlogging because they respire aerobically. Organic matter is only about 5% by volume but is responsible for a hugely disproportionate share of water-holding capacity, nutrient retention and aggregate stability: each 1% increase in soil organic matter allows roughly 15,000–25,000 extra litres of water storage per hectare in the top 30 cm.
SOIL IS ALIVE. One teaspoon (about 1 gram) of healthy topsoil contains roughly 100 million to 1 billion bacteria, several metres of fungal hyphae, thousands of protozoa, and dozens of nematodes. A hectare of good soil supports 1–2.5 tonnes of living biomass below ground — often more than the biomass above it. Earthworms alone may process 10–40 tonnes of soil per hectare per year, and their burrows create the macropores through which water infiltrates.
SOIL IS EFFECTIVELY NON-RENEWABLE on human timescales. Natural soil formation runs at roughly 0.025–0.1 mm per year — 25 to 100 mm per thousand years, or about 1 tonne per hectare per year. Global cropland erosion averages 10–40 tonnes per hectare per year. That is soil being lost 10 to 40 times faster than it is made. About 33% of the world's soils are already degraded.

sections.heading: The five soil-forming factors: CLORPT
sections.body:
Hans Jenny's 1941 state-factor equation formalised soil as a function of five independent variables: S = f(cl, o, r, p, t) — climate, organisms, relief, parent material, time.
1. CLIMATE — the dominant factor at global scale. Temperature roughly doubles reaction rates per 10 °C (the Q₁₀ rule), and water is the transport medium. Where precipitation exceeds evapotranspiration, LEACHING dominates: bases (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, K⁺) are washed down and out, leaving acidic soils. Where evapotranspiration exceeds precipitation, capillary rise dominates: salts and carbonates accumulate near the surface, giving alkaline soils and caliche/calcrete layers. Tropical soils are deeply weathered (10–30 m of saprolite) and infertile despite hosting rainforest, because nearly all nutrients are held in the living biomass, not the soil.
2. ORGANISMS — vegetation type determines organic inputs. Grassland roots die and decay throughout a deep root zone, producing thick, dark, base-rich A horizons (the mollisols of the world's grain belts, with 1–1.5 m of black topsoil). Conifer forests drop acidic litter that leaches from the top down, producing a thin, ash-grey leached horizon (spodosols). Earthworms, ants, termites and burrowing mammals mix soil (bioturbation); fungi and bacteria decompose litter; legumes with Rhizobium bacteria fix atmospheric N₂ into plant-available nitrogen at 50–300 kg N per hectare per year.
3. RELIEF (topography) — slope angle controls erosion and water residence. Steep slopes have thin, young, poorly developed soils because material is removed as fast as it forms. Footslopes and valley bottoms accumulate deep, dark, moist colluvial soils. ASPECT matters strongly in mid-latitudes: in the northern hemisphere, south-facing slopes are warmer and drier with thinner soils; north-facing slopes are cooler, moister, and often support deeper organic accumulation (reversed in the southern hemisphere).
4. PARENT MATERIAL — the mineral starting stock, either residual (weathered in place from bedrock) or transported (alluvium by rivers, colluvium by gravity, loess by wind, till by ice, volcanic ash). It sets initial texture, mineralogy and nutrient supply. Limestone weathers to clay-rich, calcium-rich, near-neutral soils; granite to sandy, acidic, quartz-rich soils; basalt to clay-rich, iron-rich, fertile soils (which is why volcanic regions such as Java and Campania are agricultural powerhouses); volcanic ash to andisols with extraordinary phosphorus fixation.
5. TIME — a soil needs centuries to millennia to develop horizons. Rough benchmarks: a recognisable A horizon in 50–200 years; a distinct B horizon in 1,000–10,000 years; a mature, fully differentiated profile in 10,000–100,000+ years. Highly weathered tropical oxisols have been developing for millions of years.

sections.heading: The four processes and the soil profile
sections.body:
Four processes act simultaneously to build horizons: ADDITIONS (organic litter, dust, rainfall, fertiliser), LOSSES (leaching, erosion, gaseous loss, plant uptake and harvest removal), TRANSLOCATIONS (movement within the profile — ELUVIATION is removal from a horizon, ILLUVIATION is accumulation in one), and TRANSFORMATIONS (weathering, humification, mineral formation).
WEATHERING supplies the mineral raw material and comes in two kinds. PHYSICAL weathering breaks rock without changing its chemistry: frost wedging (water expands 9% on freezing, generating up to 200 MPa in a confined crack — the single most effective process in cold climates, most active where temperatures oscillate across 0 °C), salt crystallisation, thermal expansion, exfoliation from unloading, root wedging, and abrasion. CHEMICAL weathering changes mineral composition: HYDROLYSIS is the most important, where feldspar plus carbonic acid becomes clay — 2KAlSi₃O₈ + 2H₂CO₃ + 9H₂O → Al₂Si₂O₅(OH)₄ (kaolinite) + 4H₄SiO₄ + 2K⁺ + 2HCO₃⁻; OXIDATION rusts iron-bearing minerals (4FeO + O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃), giving soils their red and yellow colours; CARBONATION dissolves limestone (CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2HCO₃⁻), which is what makes caves; HYDRATION and biological chelation by root and lichen acids round it out. Physical weathering accelerates chemical weathering by multiplying surface area: splitting a 1 m cube into 1 cm cubes increases surface area 100-fold.
THE SOIL PROFILE, top to bottom:
• O HORIZON — organic litter, from fresh leaves (Oi) through partly decomposed (Oe) to fully humified (Oa). Absent in most cultivated and desert soils, thick in forests and peatlands.
• A HORIZON (topsoil) — mineral soil darkened by humus, the zone of maximum biological activity and root density. Typically 5–30 cm; up to 1 m in prairie mollisols. This is the horizon that erosion takes first and that agriculture depends on.
• E HORIZON — zone of maximum ELUVIATION, leached pale grey or white because clay, iron and aluminium have been stripped out. Prominent under conifers and in sandy, high-rainfall settings.
• B HORIZON (subsoil) — zone of ILLUVIATION, where the clay, iron oxides and carbonates removed from above accumulate. Denser, often more strongly coloured (red, brown, orange), and where you see structural development like blocky or prismatic peds.
• C HORIZON — weathered parent material, only slightly altered, still recognisably the original rock or sediment.
• R HORIZON — consolidated bedrock.
To examine a profile, dig a pit at least 1 m deep with one clean vertical face (or use a road cut or stream bank), face it away from the sun to see colour without glare, and describe each horizon's depth, colour (ideally with a Munsell chart — the notation is hue value/chroma, e.g. 10YR 3/2 for a dark greyish brown), texture, structure, consistence, root abundance, and boundary sharpness.

sections.heading: Texture, structure and water: the physical properties that decide everything
sections.body:
TEXTURE is the proportion by mass of the three mineral size fractions (USDA scale): SAND 2.0–0.05 mm (gritty, visible, low surface area), SILT 0.05–0.002 mm (smooth like flour when dry, slippery when wet), CLAY under 0.002 mm (sticky, plastic, enormous surface area — clay has 10,000 to 100,000 times the surface area per gram of sand, which is why it controls chemistry). LOAM is the balanced ideal, roughly 40% sand, 40% silt, 20% clay. Texture cannot be changed by management at any realistic scale — you must work with what you have.
THE HAND TEXTURE TEST (ribbon method), a reliable field procedure:
1. Take a walnut-sized ball of soil, remove stones and roots.
2. Add water a few drops at a time and knead until it is the consistency of putty — moist enough to be plastic, not wet enough to be sticky.
3. Squeeze the ball between thumb and forefinger, pushing upward to form a ribbon that hangs over your finger. If NO ribbon forms and the soil will not hold a ball → SAND. If it forms a ball but the ribbon breaks under 2.5 cm → LOAMY SAND or LOAM. Ribbon 2.5–5 cm → CLAY LOAM. Ribbon over 5 cm before breaking → CLAY.
4. Now wet a pinch excessively and rub between fingers: distinctly GRITTY → sandy (e.g. sandy clay loam); distinctly SMOOTH/silky → silty (silty clay loam); neither dominant → the plain version (clay loam).
THE JAR TEST for quantitative texture: fill a straight-sided jar one-third with soil, add water to nearly full plus a teaspoon of dish soap as a dispersant, shake vigorously for 2 minutes, then set down. Mark the settled level after 1 minute (sand), 2 hours (sand + silt), and 48 hours (total). Calculate each fraction as a percentage of total depth and plot on the USDA soil texture triangle.
STRUCTURE is how individual particles aggregate into PEDS, bound by fungal hyphae, root exudates, microbial glues (glomalin) and clay-humus complexes. Types: granular (best for agriculture — crumbly, porous, typical of a healthy A horizon), blocky, prismatic, columnar, platy (often a sign of compaction or crusting, and it impedes water and roots), and massive or single-grain (no structure). Unlike texture, structure CAN be improved: organic matter, root growth, cover cropping and reduced tillage all build it, while compaction, excessive tillage and working wet soil destroy it.
WATER RELATIONS. SATURATION is all pores full. FIELD CAPACITY is the water remaining after free drainage stops, about −33 kPa (−0.33 bar) matric potential, reached 1–3 days after a soaking. PERMANENT WILTING POINT is −1500 kPa (−15 bar), where roots can no longer extract water. PLANT-AVAILABLE WATER = field capacity − wilting point, and it varies enormously with texture: sand holds about 60–80 mm of available water per metre of depth, loam about 150–200 mm/m, clay about 150–180 mm/m (clay holds more total water but much of it is bound too tightly to release). WORKED EXAMPLE: a crop rooting 60 cm deep in a loam has 0.6 m × 175 mm/m ≈ 105 mm of available water. If evapotranspiration is 5 mm/day and you irrigate when 50% is depleted, you must irrigate every 105 × 0.5 / 5 ≈ 10 days, applying about 52 mm. The same crop on sand (70 mm/m → 42 mm available) needs irrigating every 4 days — which is precisely why sandy soils demand frequent, light watering and clay soils infrequent, deep watering.
BULK DENSITY = mass of oven-dry soil ÷ total volume including pores, in g/cm³. Healthy loam is 1.1–1.4 g/cm³; above about 1.6 g/cm³ in loam or 1.8 in sand, roots cannot penetrate. Porosity (%) = (1 − bulk density / particle density) × 100, taking particle density as 2.65 g/cm³. A soil at 1.3 g/cm³ has porosity = (1 − 1.3/2.65) × 100 = 51%.

sections.heading: Soil chemistry: pH, cation exchange and the nutrients
sections.body:
pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen ion activity: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], where [H⁺] is in mol/L. It is logarithmic, so pH 5 is TEN times more acidic than pH 6 and one hundred times more than pH 7. Most crops do best at pH 6.0–7.0 because that is where the widest range of nutrients is simultaneously available. Below pH 5.5, aluminium and manganese become soluble and toxic to roots, and phosphorus locks up with iron and aluminium. Above pH 7.5, phosphorus locks up with calcium, and iron, manganese, zinc and boron become unavailable — the classic cause of interveinal chlorosis (yellow leaves with green veins) in alkaline soils. Note that nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are all most available around pH 6.0–7.5, while iron and manganese peak in acid soil.
ADJUSTING pH: to RAISE pH, add agricultural lime (calcium carbonate). Rough rates to raise pH by 1.0 unit over the top 15 cm: sandy soil 1.0–1.5 kg per 10 m², loam 2.0–2.5 kg per 10 m², clay 3.0–4.0 kg per 10 m². Lime is slow — apply 3–6 months ahead, incorporate, and re-test; it takes a full season to act. Use dolomitic lime if magnesium is also low. Wood ash also raises pH (roughly half the strength of lime) and adds potassium, but is caustic and easy to overdo — cap it at about 1 kg per 10 m² per year. To LOWER pH, use elemental sulphur, which soil bacteria oxidise to sulphuric acid: roughly 0.5–1.0 kg per 10 m² lowers pH by about 1 unit in sand, 1.5–2.0 kg per 10 m² in clay, over 3–12 months. Never use anything stronger; do not attempt to acidify with household acids.
CATION EXCHANGE CAPACITY (CEC) is the soil's ability to hold positively charged nutrients on negatively charged clay and humus surfaces, measured in centimoles of charge per kilogram (cmol_c/kg, equivalently meq/100 g). Typical values: sand 1–5, loam 5–15, clay 25–50, organic/peat 50–100+. High CEC means the soil is a good nutrient bank that resists leaching; low CEC (sand) means nutrients wash straight through, so fertilise little and often. The exchangeable cations, in typical order of strength of adsorption, are Al³⁺ > Ca²⁺ > Mg²⁺ > K⁺ ≈ NH₄⁺ > Na⁺ > H⁺. A well-balanced soil has base saturation around 65–80% Ca, 10–15% Mg, 2–5% K.
THE ESSENTIAL NUTRIENTS. Plants need 17 elements. From air and water: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen (about 95% of dry plant mass). MACRONUTRIENTS from soil: nitrogen (N — the engine of leafy growth and all proteins; deficiency shows as uniform yellowing of the OLDEST leaves first, because N is mobile and the plant scavenges it from old tissue), phosphorus (P — roots, flowers, seeds, and all energy transfer via ATP; deficiency shows as stunting and purple leaf tinges), potassium (K — water regulation, stomatal control, disease resistance; deficiency shows as scorched, browning leaf MARGINS on older leaves). SECONDARY: calcium (cell walls; deficiency causes blossom-end rot in tomatoes — usually an uneven-watering transport problem rather than a genuine soil shortage), magnesium (the central atom of chlorophyll; deficiency gives interveinal yellowing on older leaves), sulphur (amino acids). MICRONUTRIENTS in trace amounts: iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine, nickel. Note the diagnostic rule: MOBILE nutrients (N, P, K, Mg) show deficiency in OLD leaves first; IMMOBILE nutrients (Ca, Fe, B, S, Zn) show it in NEW growth first. Fertiliser N-P-K labelling gives percentage N, then P₂O₅, then K₂O by mass — so a 10 kg bag of 10-10-10 contains 1 kg N, 1 kg P₂O₅ (≈0.44 kg elemental P) and 1 kg K₂O (≈0.83 kg elemental K).

sections.heading: Building and keeping fertility: compost, cover crops and erosion control
sections.body:
COMPOSTING converts raw organic waste into stable humus, and the controlling variable is the CARBON-TO-NITROGEN RATIO. Target C:N of 25:1 to 30:1 in the starting mix. High-carbon "browns": dry leaves C:N ≈ 60:1, straw 80:1, sawdust 400:1, cardboard 350:1, wood chips 400:1. High-nitrogen "greens": fresh grass clippings 20:1, vegetable scraps 15:1, coffee grounds 20:1, manure 15–25:1, urine 0.8:1. A workable practical rule is 2–3 parts browns to 1 part greens BY VOLUME.
HOT COMPOST PROCEDURE:
1. Build a pile at least 1 m × 1 m × 1 m (1 m³) — smaller piles cannot retain heat.
2. Layer browns and greens in the 2–3:1 ratio, shredding material to 2–5 cm pieces to raise surface area.
3. Moisten to the "wrung-out sponge" test — squeeze a handful and one or two drops should appear, no more. Target 50–60% moisture.
4. The pile should reach 55–65 °C within 2–4 days. Sustaining 55 °C for 3 consecutive days kills most weed seeds and human pathogens; above 70 °C the beneficial microbes themselves die, so turn to cool it.
5. Turn every 3–7 days, moving the outside to the centre. Expect 5–8 turns.
6. Finished in 6–12 weeks (hot) or 6–12 months (cold, unturned). It is ready when it is dark, crumbly, smells of forest floor, and no original materials are recognisable.
TROUBLESHOOTING: ammonia smell = too much nitrogen, add browns. Rotten-egg smell = anaerobic, turn it and add bulky browns. Not heating = too dry, too small, or too little nitrogen. NEVER compost meat, dairy, oils, pet faeces from carnivores, or diseased plants in a home pile; and do not apply raw manure to soil within 90–120 days of harvesting food crops.
COVER CROPS AND GREEN MANURE: sow legumes (clover, vetch, field peas, beans) to fix 50–200 kg N/ha; sow grasses and cereals (rye, oats, barley) for biomass and deep rooting; sow brassicas (radish, mustard) to break compaction with taproots. Cut or roll before they set seed and incorporate or leave as mulch.
MULCH: a 5–10 cm layer of straw, leaves or wood chips reduces evaporation by 50–70%, suppresses weeds, moderates soil temperature by 5–10 °C, and feeds soil biology as it breaks down. Keep it a few centimetres clear of plant stems to avoid rot.
EROSION CONTROL — the single most important act of soil conservation. The Universal Soil Loss Equation, A = R·K·LS·C·P, states that annual soil loss A (t/ha/yr) depends on rainfall erosivity R, soil erodibility K, slope length and steepness LS, cover management C, and support practice P. You cannot change R or K, and LS only with earthworks — but C and P are entirely under your control, and C alone can vary by a factor of 100 between bare soil and full cover. Practical measures: (1) NEVER leave soil bare — bare soil can lose 100× more than covered soil; (2) contour ploughing across the slope rather than up and down, cutting loss by 50%; (3) terracing on slopes above about 10°; (4) strip cropping and grassed waterways; (5) windbreaks perpendicular to prevailing wind, effective for 10–20 times their height downwind; (6) no-till or reduced till, which preserves structure and the fungal network; (7) permanent vegetation on any slope above about 25%.
COMMON MISTAKES AND SAFETY. Working soil when it is wet destroys structure and creates a compacted layer that lasts years — test by squeezing a ball and dropping it from waist height: if it shatters, it is dry enough; if it stays a ball, wait. Over-tilling burns organic matter (each pass oxidises carbon) and pulverises aggregates. Over-fertilising with nitrogen leaches to groundwater as nitrate and runs off to cause algal blooms and hypoxic dead zones. Adding sand to clay in small amounts makes something close to concrete — add organic matter instead. Do not lime and add ammonium fertiliser at the same time (you lose nitrogen as ammonia gas). SAFETY: wear gloves and wash hands after handling soil, compost or manure — tetanus (ensure vaccination is current), and pathogens including E. coli, Salmonella, Listeria and Toxoplasma are real risks; avoid inhaling dry compost dust, which can carry Aspergillus and Legionella (dampen it first, work upwind, and consider a mask). Never grow food in soil that may be contaminated with lead (common near old painted buildings, old orchards and busy roads) — have it tested; if lead exceeds about 400 ppm, use raised beds with imported soil and a barrier. Do not use treated timber, railway sleepers or tyres as bed edging for food crops.

sections.heading: Soil Taxonomy: Reading a Soil's Name Like a Classification
sections.body: Soil scientists classify soils formally the way biologists classify species, and the system used across most of the world (USDA Soil Taxonomy, with the FAO's World Reference Base as the major international alternative) groups all soils into twelve orders based on diagnostic horizons and measurable properties rather than appearance alone. A handful matter enormously to daily life. Mollisols are deep, dark, organic-rich soils that form under grassland, where centuries of dying grass roots build a thick, fertile A horizon loaded with organic matter and calcium; they underlie the world's great grain belts almost without exception — the American Midwest, Ukraine's steppe, Argentina's Pampas — not a coincidence of agriculture following fertile ground so much as civilization repeatedly discovering the same physical fact independently. Oxisols sit at the other extreme: deeply weathered tropical soils, red or yellow from iron and aluminum oxide residues, found under lush rainforest — one of the great counterintuitive lessons of soil science, because despite supporting some of Earth's densest vegetation, oxisols are chemically almost sterile, with nearly all nutrients tied up in the living biomass rather than the soil. Clear the forest and the nutrient cycle breaks: without a canopy constantly cycling nutrients back through leaf litter, a cleared oxisol can lose most of its fertility within a few growing seasons, exactly why slash-and-burn tropical plots are typically abandoned after two or three years. Aridisols (desert soils with subsurface carbonate or gypsum accumulations), Alfisols (moderately weathered temperate forest soils), Spodosols (acidic, sandy soils under conifers with a bleached near-surface layer), and Histosols (organic peat and muck) round out the orders most likely to matter to anyone gardening, farming, or reading a soil survey of their own property.

sections.heading: The Nitrogen, Phosphorus and Carbon Cycles Inside the Soil
sections.body: Behind the pH numbers and nutrient totals of soil chemistry lies genuine biochemistry worth knowing, because it explains why fertilizer behaves the way it does. Atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) is triple-bonded and extremely stable; plants cannot use it directly, so it must first be 'fixed,' done biologically by Rhizobium bacteria in symbiotic root nodules on legumes (beans, peas, clover) — why a legume cover crop genuinely adds nitrogen to a field — and done industrially by the Haber-Bosch process, which combines atmospheric N₂ with hydrogen under extreme heat and pressure to make ammonia, the single invention most responsible for the 20th century's population growth. Once in the soil as ammonium (NH₄⁺), nitrogen is oxidized step by step — Nitrosomonas to nitrite (NO₂⁻), then Nitrobacter to nitrate (NO₃⁻), nitrification. Nitrate is the form roots most readily absorb, but it's negatively charged and not held by the negatively charged clay and humus dominating cation exchange capacity, so it's highly prone to leaching into groundwater or streams — the direct chemical link to eutrophication. Phosphorus behaves almost oppositely: it binds eagerly, precipitating with iron and aluminum in acidic soils or calcium in alkaline soils, which is why it's so often the limiting nutrient despite reasonable total quantities — the problem usually isn't scarcity but immobility. Carbon completes the picture: soil organic carbon derives from decomposing residue, and how fast it breaks down is governed largely by its carbon-to-nitrogen ratio. Fresh residue near 24:1 (roughly matching decomposer microbes' own body chemistry) breaks down efficiently; sawdust or straw, with a C:N ratio that can exceed 400:1, forces microbes to scavenge nitrogen from surrounding soil, temporarily starving nearby plants — nitrogen robbery, the reason fresh wood mulch tilled directly into a vegetable bed can visibly stunt the crop.

sections.heading: The Dust Bowl and the Birth of Soil Conservation Science
sections.body: The clearest historical proof that soil is a finite, losable resource came in the 1930s American and Canadian prairies. Decades of grassland had been plowed under for wheat without regard for the deep-rooted native grass cover that had held fine prairie topsoil against wind for millennia; when a multi-year drought hit, the exposed, pulverized soil had nothing left to anchor it, and immense dust storms — 'black blizzards' — stripped topsoil by the hundreds of millions of tons, in places burying fences and reducing farms to bare subsoil, with dust carried as far as ships in the Atlantic and government buildings in Washington, D.C. Soil scientist Hugh Hammond Bennett, who had argued for over a decade that American farming was causing dangerous, largely invisible erosion, seized the moment: testifying before Congress in 1935 while a dust storm from the plains happened to darken the sky over Washington that same day, he secured funding to create the Soil Conservation Service, the first federal agency in the world built specifically to combat soil erosion. Out of that came the erosion-control toolkit still taught today: contour plowing (plowing along a slope's elevation contours so each furrow acts as a small dam against runoff), shelterbelts (rows of trees as windbreaks, directly reducing wind speed at ground level), strip-cropping, and the eventual move toward no-till and cover-crop systems keeping a living root structure in the ground year-round. The core lesson: topsoil forms over centuries but can be lost in a single bad season, and fertility built up by the CLORPT factors and the four soil-forming processes described earlier in this guide is not a renewable resource on any human timescale once it's gone.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: You can run a genuinely informative soil survey of your own garden or yard with tools that mostly already exist in a kitchen and garage.
ingredients: A soil probe or a simple garden trowel/spade for extracting an intact vertical soil sample down to 20–30 cm
A clear straight-sided mason jar with a tight lid, for the soil texture settling test
A ruler for measuring settled sediment layers in the jar
A pH test kit — either simple color-change strips/capsules or an inexpensive digital soil pH meter — from a garden center or hardware store
A soil thermometer, useful for tracking when soil has warmed enough for spring planting or monitoring a compost pile's internal temperature
An empty tin can with both ends removed (or a section of PVC pipe), a rubber mallet, and a stopwatch, for a simple infiltration-rate test
Compost bin materials: a mix of 'browns' (dry leaves, straw, cardboard) and 'greens' (fresh grass clippings, vegetable scraps) plus a bin or simple wire enclosure
Work gloves, since handling soil, especially near a compost pile or manure, calls for basic hygiene precautions, and washing hands thoroughly afterward
A notebook for recording layer depths, colors (a soil color reference chart is a worthwhile inexpensive addition), and test results by location

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Run Your Own Soil Texture, pH and Infiltration Test
sections.body: These three tests together — texture, pH, and infiltration rate — tell you almost everything a gardener or small farmer actually needs to know about a patch of ground, and each takes under an hour of active work.
steps: Texture (jar test): fill a mason jar about one-third full with soil from 5–10 cm depth, add water until nearly full, add a small pinch of dish soap as a dispersant, seal tightly, and shake vigorously for 2–3 minutes to fully suspend the particles.

Set the jar level and undisturbed. Mark the sand layer that settles after exactly 1 minute, the silt layer after roughly 2 hours, and the final clay layer (still faintly cloudy) after it fully clears, which can take a day or several days — larger sand particles fall fastest under gravity while fine clay stays suspended far longer (Stokes' Law).

Measure the thickness of each layer with a ruler, calculate the percentage each represents of the total settled depth, and plot the three percentages on a standard soil texture triangle to get your texture class.

pH: follow your kit's instructions exactly, typically mixing soil with distilled water in a specified ratio and reading a color change or a digital probe; test two or three separate spots, since pH commonly varies over just a few meters.
Infiltration: drive the open tin can about 5 cm into the ground with the rubber mallet, keeping it level and not cracking the surrounding soil.
Pour a measured amount of water into the can (about 2.5 cm depth, roughly one inch) and start the stopwatch the instant you finish pouring.

Record the time for the water to fully infiltrate; repeat once more on the same spot to reduce the effect of initial dry-soil resistance, and calculate the infiltration rate in centimeters or inches per hour.

Compare your rate against reference values (well-structured loam typically infiltrates several centimeters per hour; compacted clay can be a tenth of that or less) to judge whether the soil's structure needs improvement, such as added organic matter or reduced foot/vehicle traffic.

guides.title: Reading the Landscape & Geology in the Field
guides.summary: How to interpret terrain like a geologist — the principles of relative dating, measuring strike and dip, recognising folds, faults and unconformities, decoding glacial, river, coastal and karst landforms, and using it all to find water, safe ground and useful materials.

sections.heading: The reasoning framework: how to date what you see with no instruments
sections.body:
Field geology rests on a handful of logical principles established between 1669 and 1830, and they let you order events in time using nothing but observation. Together they are called RELATIVE DATING — determining sequence, not calendar age.
• UNIFORMITARIANISM (Hutton, 1785) — "the present is the key to the past." Physical laws are constant, so the processes you can watch today (a river depositing sand, a wave rounding a pebble, a volcano erupting) explain identical features in ancient rock. This is the master principle; everything else follows.
• SUPERPOSITION (Steno, 1669) — in an undisturbed sequence of layered rocks, each bed is younger than the one below it and older than the one above. The bottom is the oldest.
• ORIGINAL HORIZONTALITY — sediment is deposited in near-horizontal layers under gravity. So tilted or folded beds have been deformed AFTER deposition, and the amount of tilt measures the deformation.
• LATERAL CONTINUITY — a bed extends in all directions until it thins to nothing or hits the edge of the basin. Matching beds on opposite sides of a valley means one continuous unit later cut by erosion.
• CROSS-CUTTING RELATIONSHIPS — any feature that cuts across another is younger than what it cuts. A fault that offsets a bed postdates the bed; a dyke that slices a granite postdates the granite; a fracture filled with quartz postdates the fracture.
• INCLUSIONS — fragments contained within a rock are older than the rock containing them. Granite pebbles inside a sandstone mean the granite existed first; sandstone fragments frozen into a granite mean the sandstone came first.
• BAKED AND CHILLED CONTACTS — an intrusion bakes the rock it invades (a metamorphic halo) and chills against it (fine-grained margins). Find a baked contact and you know the intrusion is younger. If instead the "intrusion" is overlain by an unbaked bed containing its fragments, it is a buried lava flow and is older.
• FAUNAL SUCCESSION (Smith, 1815) — fossil assemblages succeed one another in a definite, recognisable order worldwide, so distinctive short-lived, widespread fossils (INDEX FOSSILS such as trilobites for the Cambrian–Permian, ammonites for the Mesozoic, graptolites for the Ordovician–Silurian) date and correlate rocks between continents.
WORKED EXAMPLE — read this cliff. From the bottom: horizontal limestone; above it tilted sandstone; a granite body cutting both, with a baked halo; a basalt dyke cutting the granite; and a horizontal gravel capping everything, containing granite pebbles. Sequence: (1) limestone deposited; (2) sandstone deposited on it, then both tilted; (3) granite intruded (cross-cutting + baking); (4) dyke intruded (cuts granite); (5) uplift and erosion levelled the surface; (6) gravel deposited (superposition, and its granite pebbles confirm the granite was already exposed). Six events, no equipment, pure logic.

sections.heading: Structure: strike, dip, folds and faults
sections.body:
STRIKE and DIP describe the orientation of any planar feature — a bedding plane, a fault, a joint, a foliation. STRIKE is the compass bearing of the horizontal line formed where the plane intersects a horizontal surface. DIP is the angle, measured in the vertical plane perpendicular to strike, between the plane and horizontal, from 0° (flat) to 90° (vertical). Dip direction is always 90° from strike; you must also record which way it dips (e.g. "strike 045°, dip 30° SE").
MEASURING WITHOUT A GEOLOGICAL COMPASS: (1) For strike, place a water bottle on the bed surface, or trickle water on it and mark the horizontal line where the water does NOT run (water runs directly down dip, so the line perpendicular to its flow, in the plane, is strike). Sight along that line with any compass. (2) For dip, hold a smartphone flat against the bed perpendicular to strike and read its inclinometer, or make a simple clinometer: a protractor with a weighted string hanging from its centre, held with one straight edge against the rock — the string reads the complement of the angle. Always take three or more readings on different parts of a bed and average them; a single reading on a lumpy surface can be 10° out.
FOLDS form under compression, in ductile conditions (deeper, warmer, slower strain). An ANTICLINE arches upward with the OLDEST rocks in the core; a SYNCLINE troughs downward with the YOUNGEST rocks in the core. This age criterion, not the surface shape, is the definition, because erosion can leave an anticline as a valley and a syncline as a ridge (INVERTED RELIEF). Parts of a fold: the AXIAL PLANE divides it symmetrically; the HINGE is the line of maximum curvature; the LIMBS are the flanks. A fold is symmetric, asymmetric, overturned (one limb rotated past vertical) or recumbent (axial plane near-horizontal) — and increasing asymmetry indicates increasing strain and tells you the direction the compression came from, because folds "lean away" from the push. A MONOCLINE is a single step-like bend. In map view, eroded plunging folds make distinctive V or hairpin outcrop patterns: an eroded plunging anticline's beds V in the direction of plunge; a syncline's V opposite.
FAULTS form under brittle conditions (shallow, cooler, faster strain). The HANGING WALL lies above an inclined fault plane; the FOOTWALL below (the old miner's terms: you hang your lamp on one and stand on the other).
• NORMAL fault — hanging wall moves DOWN. Caused by EXTENSION (tension). Produces horsts (upthrown blocks) and grabens (downdropped blocks), rift valleys, and Basin-and-Range topography. The crust is stretched and lengthened.
• REVERSE fault — hanging wall moves UP. Caused by COMPRESSION. A THRUST fault is a reverse fault with a dip under 30°, which can push older rock over younger for tens of kilometres — the single most common way superposition appears violated.
• STRIKE-SLIP fault — horizontal motion, no vertical component. Described as right-lateral (dextral) or left-lateral (sinistral) by which way the far side appears to move as you face the fault. The San Andreas is right-lateral.
FIELD EVIDENCE OF FAULTING even when displacement is not visible: SLICKENSIDES (polished, grooved fault surfaces — the grooves give the slip direction), fault BRECCIA and GOUGE (crushed and powdered rock in the fault zone), abrupt truncation of beds, repeated or missing stratigraphy in a section, springs aligned in a straight line, an abnormally straight valley or scarp, and offset streams or ridges.
JOINTS are fractures with NO displacement, and they matter practically far more than their subtlety suggests: they control where water enters rock, where weathering attacks, where cliffs fail, and how quarried blocks split. Columnar jointing (the hexagonal columns of the Giant's Causeway) forms by contraction as thick lava cools; sheeting joints form parallel to the surface as overburden is removed and granite expands, producing the domes of Yosemite.

sections.heading: Unconformities and reading a landscape's missing time
sections.body:
An UNCONFORMITY is a buried erosional or non-depositional surface — a gap in the rock record, representing time for which no rock is preserved at that location. Recognising them is the single most powerful skill in reconstructing a region's history, because each one records a full cycle of uplift, erosion and re-submergence.
• ANGULAR UNCONFORMITY — tilted or folded beds overlain by horizontal beds. Sequence: deposition → tilting/folding (tectonism) → uplift → erosion to a flat surface → subsidence → new deposition. Hutton's Unconformity at Siccar Point, Scotland, is the type example: near-vertical Silurian greywacke overlain by gently dipping Devonian Old Red Sandstone, with about 65 million years missing — the observation that convinced Hutton of "no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end."
• DISCONFORMITY — an erosional surface between PARALLEL beds. Harder to spot: look for an irregular, channelled contact, a lag of pebbles or a soil/palaeosol horizon, boreholes or burrows into the lower unit, and above all a jump in fossil assemblages. This is where index fossils earn their keep.
• NONCONFORMITY — sedimentary rocks resting directly on igneous or metamorphic basement. The Great Unconformity in the Grand Canyon separates 1.7-billion-year-old Vishnu Schist from the 525-million-year-old Tapeats Sandstone — over a billion years of rock simply absent.
• PARACONFORMITY — a gap with no visible erosion; detectable only by dating or fossils.
WORKED READING OF A CANYON WALL. In the Grand Canyon you can read almost the whole method in one view: horizontal Palaeozoic strata (superposition and original horizontality), the tilted Grand Canyon Supergroup beneath them (an angular unconformity — a mountain-building event, then planation), the crystalline Vishnu Schist at the base (a nonconformity — ancient roots of a Precambrian mountain range), all cut vertically by the Colorado River (cross-cutting — the incision is the youngest event of all). The alternating cliffs and slopes are DIFFERENTIAL EROSION: resistant limestone and sandstone stand as cliffs; weak shale and mudstone retreat as slopes. Once you internalise that rule, you can read rock strength straight off a distant hillside profile without touching it — every cliff band is a resistant unit, every bench or vegetated slope a weak one.

sections.heading: Surface processes: reading rivers, glaciers, coasts, deserts and karst
sections.body:
Landforms are diagnostic of the process that made them, and each process leaves a signature you can read from a ridge top.
FLUVIAL (river): a V-SHAPED valley cross-section means active downcutting by water. Upper reaches show steep gradients, rapids, waterfalls at resistant beds, and interlocking spurs. Middle reaches meander with cut banks and point bars. Lower reaches show broad floodplains, natural levees, oxbow lakes, and finally deltas. TERRACES — flat benches perched above the modern floodplain — are former floodplains left stranded by renewed incision, and they record either uplift or a fall in base level. ALLUVIAL FANS build where a confined mountain stream debouches onto a plain and drops its load. Drainage patterns map the underlying geology: DENDRITIC (branching like a tree) means uniform, flat-lying rock; TRELLIS (parallel main streams with right-angled tributaries) means alternating hard and soft tilted beds — classic folded mountains; RADIAL means a cone (volcano or dome); RECTANGULAR means jointed or faulted bedrock; DERANGED means recently glaciated ground.
GLACIAL: a U-SHAPED valley with a flat floor and steep walls is the unmistakable signature of ice, which scours the full valley width rather than cutting a channel. Look also for CIRQUES (armchair hollows at valley heads), ARÊTES (knife-edge ridges between cirques), HORNS (pyramidal peaks, e.g. the Matterhorn), HANGING VALLEYS (tributary valleys left high above the main valley floor, so their streams enter as waterfalls), ROCHES MOUTONNÉES (bedrock knobs smoothed and gently sloping on the upstream side, plucked and steep on the downstream side — they give ice-flow direction), STRIATIONS (parallel scratches, also giving flow direction), ERRATICS (boulders of a rock type foreign to the area), MORAINES (ridges of unsorted till — terminal, lateral, medial, recessional), DRUMLINS (streamlined egg-shaped hills, blunt end upstream), ESKERS (sinuous gravel ridges from subglacial streams), and KETTLE lakes (hollows where buried ice blocks melted). The diagnostic deposit is TILL: completely unsorted and unstratified, everything from clay to boulders jumbled together — no water could do that.
COASTAL: erosional coasts show headlands and bays (differential erosion of hard and soft rock), wave-cut platforms and notches, sea caves that become arches that collapse into stacks. Depositional coasts show beaches, spits (built by longshore drift, which is the zigzag transport of sediment by waves approaching at an angle), tombolos, barrier islands and lagoons. EMERGENT coasts (relative sea-level fall or land uplift) show raised beaches and marine terraces; SUBMERGENT coasts show rias (drowned river valleys) and fjords (drowned glacial valleys).
ARID: mechanical weathering and wind dominate. Look for VENTIFACTS (wind-faceted stones), DESERT PAVEMENT (a mosaic of interlocked stones left when fines blow away), DESERT VARNISH (a dark manganese-iron coating taking thousands of years to form — its presence indicates a long-undisturbed surface), YARDANGS, BARCHAN dunes (crescents with horns pointing DOWNWIND, in limited-sand areas) and transverse or star dunes, INSELBERGS, MESAS, BUTTES, and PLAYAS (dry lakebeds with salt crusts). Wadis and arroyos are dry most of the year and are the sites of flash floods.
KARST (soluble rock, mostly limestone and gypsum): sinkholes/dolines, disappearing streams, dry valleys, caves, springs and resurgences, limestone pavement with clints (blocks) and grikes (fissures), and towers. Karst has a distinct hydrology — water moves fast through conduits with almost no filtration — with the practical consequences that surface streams are scarce, groundwater is abundant but easily contaminated, and the ground can collapse.
MASS MOVEMENT: creep (bent tree trunks curving upslope at the base, tilted fences and poles, bulging retaining walls), solifluction lobes, slumps (rotational, leaving a curved scarp at the head and a bulging toe), earthflows and mudflows, debris flows, rockfall (talus/scree cones at cliff bases), and avalanches. The stability rule of thumb is the FACTOR OF SAFETY, FS = resisting forces ÷ driving forces; failure when FS < 1. The angle of repose for dry loose material is 30–37°; add water and it can fail below 15°, because water adds weight and raises pore pressure, which reduces the effective stress holding grains together.

sections.heading: Practical field method: what to carry and how to work a site
sections.body:
KIT (a complete, compact set):
• Hand lens, 10× — the single most useful item; it turns "grey rock" into identifiable minerals.
• Geological hammer (a square-head 500–1000 g for sedimentary rock, a pick-end for hard rock) and a cold chisel. NEVER an ordinary claw hammer — the hardened striking face is not designed for rock and can spall.
• Safety glasses. Non-negotiable.
• Compass with clinometer, or a phone with a compass and inclinometer app (check declination — magnetic north differs from true north by up to 20°+ depending on where you are, and the correction changes over years).
• Streak plate, pocket knife, magnet, dilute (5%) HCl or vinegar in a dropper bottle.
• Notebook (waterproof paper), pencil (ink runs), and a scale for photos (a coin, a ruler, a hammer).
• GPS or map and the ability to take a bearing; a small tape measure.
• Sample bags and a marker.
SITE PROCEDURE:
1. STAND BACK FIRST. Before touching anything, look at the whole exposure from a distance. Identify the major units, their attitudes, and the boundaries. Most beginners bury their nose in one rock and miss the structure.
2. SKETCH before you photograph. Sketching forces you to decide what matters; a photo lets you postpone thinking. Annotate with a scale, a north arrow, and the location.
3. Work bottom to top through a section, logging each unit: thickness, lithology, grain size, colour (fresh and weathered), sedimentary or metamorphic structures, fossils, and the nature of each contact (sharp, gradational, erosional, faulted).
4. Measure strike and dip on each mappable surface; take at least three readings.
5. Always break to a FRESH surface for identification — weathering rinds lie about colour, hardness and composition.
6. Record what you actually observe SEPARATELY from what you interpret. Write "dark, fine-grained, no visible crystals, vesicular top" as observation, and "probably a basalt flow" as interpretation. Interpretations get revised; observations do not.
7. Sample sparingly. Take a fist-sized piece from float or scree where possible rather than damaging an outcrop, label immediately, and record the exact location.
ESTIMATING SCALE AND DISTANCE WITHOUT INSTRUMENTS: your outstretched thumb subtends about 2° (roughly 35 m at 1 km); a fist at arm's length about 10°; a hand span about 20°. Pace-counting: calibrate your double-pace over a measured 100 m (typically 60–65 double paces for an adult), then count. For a cliff height, use similar triangles: hold a stick vertically at arm's length, align its top with the cliff top and your thumb with the base, then walk until stick length equals cliff height, or use a clinometer — height = distance × tan(angle) + eye height.

sections.heading: Applying it: water, safe ground, hazards and materials
sections.body:
FINDING WATER FROM GEOLOGY. Springs occur where a permeable unit overlies an impermeable one and the contact daylights on a slope — so walk the base of every sandstone or limestone cliff where it meets shale. Faults often channel water to the surface, so aligned springs mark a fault trace. In limestone country, seek resurgences at the foot of hills; in volcanic terrain, water emerges at the base of lava flows where they rest on soil or ash. Alluvium in a valley floor holds water even when the surface stream is dry — dig on the outside of the last bend in a dry channel. Vegetation is a geological map you can read from a distance: a dark green line across a hillside is a seep; phreatophytes (willow, cottonwood, sycamore, cattail, reeds) mark shallow water. Conversely, a broad, gently sloping, well-vegetated area on granite is likely a fracture zone.
CHOOSING SAFE GROUND FOR A CAMP OR STRUCTURE. AVOID: the base of any cliff or steep slope, especially where fresh talus, a scar of bare soil, or scattered angular blocks show recent rockfall; any channel, wadi, arroyo, gully or dry streambed, and the mouth of any canyon (flash floods arrive with no local rain and no warning — a rainstorm 30 km upstream can send a wall of water down a dry wash); alluvial fans (they exist because debris flows repeatedly come down them); the inside of a river bend is depositional and safer than the outside cut bank; the toe of any slope with bent trees, tilted poles, arcuate cracks, hummocky ground or a bulging base — those are creep and slump indicators; and undercut riverbanks. PREFER: level, elevated ground on bedrock or a stable terrace, with a clear view of the slope above, at least 30 m above and 100 m lateral of any drainage in flash-flood country, and out from under dead limbs.
RECOGNISING HAZARD IN THE ROCK ITSELF. Beds dipping OUT of a slope (parallel to the hillside, daylighting) are far more failure-prone than beds dipping INTO the slope — this single relationship explains a large fraction of road-cut landslides. Clay-rich or shale units are the classic slip surfaces, especially when wet. Freshly exposed faces after rain, and after freeze-thaw nights, drop rock. Overhangs and undercut faces fail without warning.
USEFUL MATERIALS FROM THE FIELD. CLAY for pottery or sealing: find it in river banks, pond bottoms and B horizons; test by rolling a 5 mm coil and bending it around your finger — if it holds without cracking, it is usable. Clean it by SLAKING (dry it, break it up, cover with water, let it disperse, pour off the fine suspension, and let that settle — the settled fines are your clay). SAND AND GRAVEL for filtration and construction from riverbeds and terraces; well-sorted is best for filtration. LIMESTONE can be burnt to quicklime at 900 °C (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂) and slaked to lime mortar — this is genuinely hazardous, as quicklime reacts violently and exothermically with water and causes severe alkali burns to skin and eyes, so treat it with the same caution as strong caustic. FLINT AND CHERT from limestone nodules for sparks and cutting edges — strike flint against high-carbon steel, not stainless. QUARTZITE and dense igneous rock for hearth stones (never porous or water-soaked rock — trapped water flashes to steam and can spall it explosively). OCHRE (iron oxide) for pigment from weathered iron-rich zones. SALT from evaporite deposits and playa crusts, though playa crusts frequently contain sodium carbonate, sulphate or borate rather than sodium chloride and can be genuinely harmful — do not assume a white crust is table salt.
COMMON MISTAKES AND SAFETY. Do not trust colour alone for identification; do not identify from a weathered surface; do not confuse metamorphic foliation with sedimentary bedding (foliation cuts across bedding and is defined by aligned mica, not by grain-size change); do not assume every dark fine-grained rock is basalt (it may be a fine-grained sedimentary rock, a hornfels or a chert); and do not assume a layered outcrop is right-way-up — check for way-up indicators such as graded bedding (coarse at base), cross-bed truncation (truncated at the top), ripple crests (pointing up), mud cracks (V narrowing downward) and load casts. SAFETY: wear eye protection and a helmet under any face; never work alone in remote terrain or tell nobody your route; avoid road cuts on live roads and always assume a quarry face is unstable; stay out of abandoned mines and adits entirely (bad air, unstable ground, vertical winzes concealed under debris); watch tides and the retreat route on coastal sections; avoid inhaling rock dust; check land ownership and legal collecting rules before you remove anything; and remember that the great majority of geological field accidents are ordinary — slips, falls, dehydration and exposure — not exotic.

sections.heading: Topographic Maps and Cross-Sections: Turning Contour Lines Into 3-D Structure
sections.body: A topographic map is a geologist's first and best instrument, because contour lines encode three-dimensional shape on a flat page, letting you infer subsurface structure before swinging a hammer. The rule of Vs is the single most useful pattern: where a contour line crosses a stream valley, it always points upstream, forming a V that opens downhill — because the valley floor is lower than the surrounding ground on both sides, a contour tracing constant elevation has to dip upstream to stay level as it crosses the drainage. The same logic extends to reading a tilted, dipping rock layer's outcrop pattern as it crosses topography: where a dipping bed crosses a valley, its outcrop trace also forms a V, pointing in the dip direction if the dip is steeper than the valley's slope, and opposite the dip direction if the dip is gentler than the slope — a subtlety worth working through slowly with a real example rather than memorizing blind. From a strike-and-dip measurement at a single outcrop plus surrounding topography, a geologist constructs a cross-section: draw a vertical slice along a chosen line, project the elevation profile from the contours onto it, then use trigonometry to project the rock layer's position underground. One correction is essential: if your cross-section line isn't perpendicular to the strike, you're seeing an apparent dip rather than true dip, related by tan(apparent dip) = tan(true dip) × cos(angle between the section line and strike) — apparent dip is always shallower, and ignoring this is one of the most common errors in a first geologic cross-section.

sections.heading: Aerial and Satellite Reconnaissance: Reading a Landscape From Above
sections.body: Long before setting a boot on the ground, a field geologist typically studies a location from above — historically aerial photographs, now routinely satellite imagery and digital elevation models — because certain structural and process clues are far easier to see at a landscape scale. Drainage patterns are diagnostic: a dendritic pattern, branching irregularly like a tree, indicates fairly uniform, undeformed rock; a trellis pattern, long parallel main streams joined by short right-angle tributaries, indicates folded sedimentary rock with alternating resistant and weak layers channeling drainage; a radial pattern, streams flowing outward from a central point, indicates a volcanic cone or dome; a rectangular pattern, frequent right-angle bends, indicates bedrock cut by a grid of intersecting joints or faults water preferentially erodes along. Straight-line features cutting across a landscape — a linear valley segment, an abrupt vegetation or drainage change, aligned sag ponds — are called lineaments, and while not every lineament is a fault, a fault nearly always produces one, making lineament-mapping a standard first step in siting anything from a dam to a power plant, precisely to screen for unrecognized active faults nearby. Vegetation itself is a geological proxy: plant communities are often sharply zoned by underlying soil chemistry and drainage, so a mappable line where forest type changes abruptly, or a patch of stressed or unusually vigorous vegetation, frequently traces a real change in rock type, soil depth, or even a buried fault. None of this replaces ground-truthing, but starting from above turns a blind traverse into a targeted one.

sections.heading: Case Study: Reading Two Billion Years From the Walls of the Grand Canyon
sections.body: The Grand Canyon teaches field geology precisely because the Colorado River did the excavation for you, exposing nearly two billion years of history in a mile-deep cliff face readable top to bottom using nothing but the principles already covered. At the bottom sits the Vishnu Basement Rocks, roughly 1.75 billion years old, deeply metamorphosed schist and gneiss intruded by younger granite — rock once buried many kilometers deep, heated, and squeezed long before anything resembling the canyon existed. Above it sits the Great Unconformity, one of Earth's most famous unconformities: a gap spanning up to 1.2 billion years in places, representing rock once above the basement being entirely stripped away by erosion, leaving no record — reading the contact, you go directly from ancient metamorphic basement to much younger sedimentary rock with essentially nothing recorded between, a silence longer than the entire time multicellular life has existed. Above the unconformity comes a stack of Paleozoic sedimentary layers — the Tapeats Sandstone (a shoreline deposit marking an ancient sea advancing), the Bright Angel Shale, the Muav Limestone, and higher the Redwall Limestone, Supai Group, and Coconino Sandstone (fossilized ancient sand dunes with preserved cross-bedding and reptile trackways) — each layer's grain size, structures, and fossils telling a specific story of shifting shorelines over roughly 300 million years, using exactly the same environmental-inference logic covered for sedimentary rocks and unconformities. The canyon itself is geologically almost an afterthought — cut by the Colorado River only within the last five or six million years — a reminder of how different the timescales of rock formation and landscape carving really are: the walls record two billion years, but the shape you're standing in front of is barely older than the human genus.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: A field kit for structural geology is compact enough to fit in a daypack, and every item on this list earns its place.
ingredients: A geologic/Brunton-style compass, or at minimum a reliable magnetic compass plus a clinometer/inclinometer app on a smartphone, for measuring strike and dip

A rock hammer with a flat striking face and, ideally, a pointed pick end, plus safety glasses whenever striking rock (chips fly, and eye injuries from rock splinters are the single most common field-geology injury)
A 10x hand lens or loupe on a cord around your neck, for grain-size and mineral identification in the field
A waterproof field notebook and a set of mechanical pencils (ink runs in rain; pencil doesn't)
A topographic map of the area, printed or on an offline-capable mapping app, plus a GPS unit or smartphone for recording precise outcrop locations
Small sample bags with a permanent marker for labeling each specimen with location and a field number matching your notebook
A dropper bottle of dilute hydrochloric acid for spot-testing carbonates, used carefully with the safety glasses already on hand

Sturdy ankle-supporting boots, work gloves, a basic first aid kit, and enough water and sun protection for the planned traverse — most field-geology injuries are sprained ankles and heat exhaustion, not falling rock, and both are entirely preventable with basic preparation

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Measure Strike and Dip and Log a Real Outcrop
sections.body: This is the single most fundamental field skill in structural geology — once you can do this reliably, every fold and fault map in a textbook stops being abstract.
steps: Find a clean, reasonably flat exposure of a bedding plane, foliation surface, or other planar rock feature, brushing away loose debris or lichen if needed.

To measure strike: hold the compass's straight edge flat against the rock surface, level the compass's bubble by tilting the compass (not the rock), and read the bearing along the edge — this is the strike, the compass direction of the horizontal line where the tilted plane intersects an imaginary horizontal surface.
Record the strike as a bearing (e.g., '040°' or 'N40°E') in your notebook, along with the outcrop's GPS coordinates and a field ID number.

To measure dip: rotate the compass 90° from the strike direction so its edge points in the direction the layer is tilting downward, hold the clinometer function against the rock surface along that line, and read the angle from horizontal.
Record the dip as degrees plus a general compass direction of tilt (e.g., '42° SE'), giving you full strike-and-dip notation together, such as '040°, 42° SE.'

Sketch a simple cross-section or plan-view diagram in your notebook, marking the strike-and-dip symbol (a T-shape: the long line along strike, the short perpendicular tick pointing in the dip direction, labeled with the dip angle) exactly as it would appear on a published geologic map.

Describe the rock from bottom to top if multiple layers are visible: grain size, color, sedimentary or metamorphic structures, approximate thickness, and any fossils, using the identification skills from the rock-cycle guide.

Collect a labeled sample only if needed for later reference (many sites discourage or restrict sampling — check first), then repeat the strike-and-dip measurement at two or three more points along the same layer before leaving, since a single measurement can be a local anomaly, and a consistent set of readings gives real confidence in the structure's true orientation.

guides.title: Earth's Climate System — The Planetary Heat Engine
guides.summary: How incoming sunlight, the greenhouse effect, atmospheric circulation, and ocean currents together set Earth's average temperature — and what actually nudges that balance over decades, as distinct from day-to-day weather.

sections.heading: Weather Is One Roll of the Dice; Climate Is the Casino's Odds
sections.body:
Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a particular place and moment: today's temperature, this afternoon's rain, the gust that just moved the trees. It is governed by chaotic, non-linear fluid dynamics, which is why forecasts degrade steadily and reliably fall apart beyond roughly ten to fourteen days no matter how good the model or how dense the observations. The reason is not ignorance but sensitivity to initial conditions, the property Edward Lorenz stumbled on in 1961 when restarting a simulation from a printout rounded to three decimal places produced a completely different forecast within two simulated months. Because the atmosphere's true state is only ever known approximately, tiny measurement errors grow exponentially, doubling roughly every day or two, until they swamp the signal.

Climate is a different quantity entirely: the statistical distribution of weather over a long period, conventionally averaged over thirty years by the World Meteorological Organization, which publishes standard normals for 1961-1990, 1991-2020 and so on. Thirty years is not arbitrary. It is long enough to average out the year-to-year noise of individual storms and El Nino events, and short enough that the statistics still describe a recognisable present rather than an era. A single cold snap or a record snowfall is one roll of the dice; climate change is a change in the odds behind every subsequent roll. The mean shifts, and so does the frequency of extremes at both tails, and the two effects are not symmetric.

That asymmetry is worth making concrete, because it is the part people find least intuitive. If daily temperature maxima at a location are roughly normally distributed with a standard deviation of about 3 degrees Celsius, shifting the whole distribution warmer by just 1 degree, a third of a standard deviation, roughly doubles the frequency of days that previously counted as extreme heat at the two-sigma threshold, while cutting the frequency of extreme cold days by a comparable factor. A small shift in the average produces a large change in the tails. This is why the honest phrasing in attribution science is probabilistic: a specific heatwave is not caused by warming in the way a match causes a fire, but its likelihood may have risen by a factor that can be estimated from model ensembles run with and without human forcing.

The distinction sounds pedantic until you notice how often it is skipped. The objection that heavy snow this winter disproves warming conflates one observation with a shift in a thirty-year mean. Both a warmer average and an occasional record cold snap are fully compatible outcomes of the same shifted distribution; a shifted bell curve still has a left tail. The reverse error is equally common, treating a single hot summer as proof. Neither single event, warm or cold, carries much information. The signal lives in the distribution, which is why the discipline depends on multi-decade records kept with consistent instruments at consistent locations, and why breaks in those records are treated as a serious problem requiring careful statistical correction rather than a nuisance.

sections.heading: The Energy Budget: What Comes In Must (Eventually) Go Out
sections.body:
Start at the top of the atmosphere, because that is the only boundary across which Earth exchanges energy with the rest of the universe in any meaningful quantity. The Sun delivers about 1,361 watts per square metre to a surface held perpendicular to the beam at Earth's mean orbital distance, a quantity called the total solar irradiance or, historically, the solar constant. It is not quite constant: it varies by roughly 0.1 percent over the eleven-year sunspot cycle, and by about 6.9 percent between perihelion in early January and aphelion in early July, because Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical.

That figure applies to a disc facing the Sun, but Earth is a rotating sphere. The planet intercepts sunlight over its cross-sectional area, which is a circle of area pi times the radius squared, while it emits and receives across its full surface area of four pi times the radius squared, exactly four times larger. Averaged over the whole planet and the whole day-night cycle, incoming sunlight is therefore 1,361 divided by 4, about 340 watts per square metre. Committing that factor of four to memory resolves a great deal of confusion, because it is why the globally averaged solar input is a few hundred watts per square metre rather than the far larger number a midday reading suggests.

Of those 340 watts per square metre, roughly 30 percent is reflected straight back to space without ever warming anything. That fraction is Earth's albedo, and it is not a single surface property but a sum of contributions: clouds return roughly 20 percentage points of it, the atmosphere and its aerosols scatter a few more, and bright ground surfaces, principally snow and ice, account for the remainder. Fresh snow reflects 80 to 90 percent of the light falling on it, desert sand around 30 to 40 percent, forest canopy 10 to 15 percent, and open ocean under a high sun only 5 to 10 percent. Because clouds dominate, the planetary albedo is far more sensitive to cloud cover than to any land change, and cloud response remains the largest single uncertainty in climate projection.

The remaining 240 watts per square metre is absorbed, and in a steady climate exactly that much must be radiated back to space as longwave infrared, or the planet accumulates or loses heat until balance is restored. This is simply conservation of energy applied to a planet. The crucial asymmetry is spectral: sunlight arrives mostly as visible and near-infrared radiation because the Sun's surface is near 5,800 kelvin, while Earth radiates in the thermal infrared around 10 micrometres because its surface is near 288 kelvin. The two streams barely overlap in wavelength, which is precisely what allows a gas to be transparent to one and opaque to the other. That absorbed-shortwave-in, emitted-longwave-out balance is the entire budget the rest of the climate system exists to move around and, in the case of greenhouse gases, temporarily hold onto. A persistent imbalance of even one watt per square metre, currently measured at roughly 0.5 to 1, means the planet is accumulating energy, most of which goes into the ocean.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Earth's Temperature With and Without a Blanket
sections.body:
The Stefan-Boltzmann law states that a perfect blackbody radiates energy at a rate equal to sigma times temperature to the fourth power, where sigma is 5.67 times ten to the minus eighth watts per square metre per kelvin to the fourth. Setting that equal to the 240 watts per square metre Earth must emit and solving gives a temperature of 240 divided by 5.67 times ten to the minus eight, all raised to the power one quarter, which is about 255 kelvin, or minus 18 degrees Celsius. That is Earth's effective radiating temperature, roughly the figure you would calculate for an airless rock of the same reflectivity at our distance from the Sun. The fourth-power dependence matters in itself: a one percent change in absolute temperature changes emitted power by four percent, which makes radiation an extremely stiff restoring force.

The actual global mean surface temperature is about 288 kelvin, 15 degrees Celsius, a full 33 degrees warmer than the calculation predicts. That 33-degree gap is the greenhouse effect, and the mechanism is specific rather than vague. Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone are largely transparent to incoming visible sunlight but absorb strongly in the thermal infrared, because molecules absorb radiation only at wavelengths matching their vibrational and rotational transitions. This is also why the two dominant constituents of the atmosphere are irrelevant here: nitrogen and oxygen are symmetric diatomic molecules with no permanent dipole moment, so they have no infrared absorption bands worth the name. A gas needs three or more atoms, or at least an asymmetric charge distribution, to interact with infrared at all.

The correct picture is not a literal blanket but an altitude shift. Adding an absorbing gas raises the effective emission level, the altitude from which infrared photons finally escape to space without being reabsorbed. That level must still sit at about 255 kelvin, because the energy budget requires it. Since temperature falls with height through the troposphere at roughly 6.5 degrees per kilometre, a higher emission level implies a warmer surface underneath it. Adding carbon dioxide raises that level by a few hundred metres, and the surface must warm to keep the escape altitude at the required temperature. The lapse rate is therefore as essential to the mechanism as the absorption itself; on a planet with an isothermal atmosphere, greenhouse gases would have almost no surface effect.

The 33-degree figure is a fair headline but hides a subtlety worth stating. It compares present Earth with a hypothetical Earth retaining today's 30 percent albedo but no absorbing gases. A genuinely greenhouse-free Earth would freeze over, its albedo would climb toward 0.6 or higher as ice spread, and the equilibrium would land nearer minus 50 degrees Celsius. Attribution among the gases is also not additive, because their absorption bands overlap; water vapour contributes roughly half and carbon dioxide about a fifth, with the ranges depending on how the overlap is apportioned. Crucially, water vapour is a feedback rather than a driver, since its concentration is set by temperature.

sections.heading: The Real Engine: The Tropics-to-Poles Temperature Gradient
sections.body:
Because Earth is a sphere rather than a flat disc facing the Sun, sunlight strikes the tropics nearly head-on and the poles at a grazing angle. The geometry is exact: the energy per unit ground area scales with the cosine of the angle between the incoming beam and the local vertical. At solar noon on an equinox the Sun is directly overhead at the equator, cosine equals one, and full intensity lands on the ground; at 60 degrees latitude the same beam arrives at 60 degrees from vertical, cosine equals a half, and the identical energy is smeared over twice the area. Think of a torch beam hitting a wall square on versus at a sharp angle. Averaged over a full year, including the compensating effect of long polar summer days, the equatorial zone still receives roughly two to two and a half times the solar energy per square metre that the poles do.

A second, smaller effect works in the same direction. Light arriving obliquely traverses a longer slant path through the atmosphere, so more of it is scattered or absorbed before reaching the surface, and it lands preferentially on the brightest surfaces on the planet, the polar snow and sea ice, which reflect most of what does arrive. Absorbed energy at high latitudes is therefore reduced twice over, by geometry and by albedo.

The consequence is a permanent energy surplus in the tropics and a permanent deficit near the poles. Satellite radiation budget measurements put the crossover at roughly 35 to 40 degrees latitude in each hemisphere: equatorward of that line the planet absorbs more sunlight than it radiates to space, poleward of it the reverse. If nothing carried heat between the two regions, the tropics would warm and the poles cool without limit until each reached its own local radiative equilibrium, giving a tropical surface somewhere above 40 degrees Celsius and polar regions far colder than they are.

They do not, because the atmosphere and ocean exist, from an energy standpoint, precisely to erase that imbalance. The required poleward transport peaks at roughly 5.5 to 6 petawatts in each hemisphere near 35 degrees latitude, a number worth pausing on: it is about three hundred times total human primary energy consumption. Every hurricane, every jet stream meander, every mid-latitude depression and every ocean current is, from this point of view, a heat-transport mechanism working to flatten a gradient that solar geometry keeps recreating. This reframes weather itself. A storm is not an anomaly interrupting the system; it is the system doing its job, and mid-latitude weather is chaotic mainly because the poleward transport there is accomplished by discrete travelling eddies rather than by a steady overturning. The gradient also explains a robust projection: because the Arctic is warming several times faster than the tropics, the equator-to-pole temperature difference is shrinking, which weakens the thermal driving of the mid-latitude circulation, though exactly how the resulting weather patterns respond remains genuinely contested among researchers.

sections.heading: Atmospheric Circulation: Hadley, Ferrel, and Polar Cells
sections.body:
Each hemisphere organises its poleward heat transport into three great overturning cells, and the reason there are three rather than one is Earth's rotation. On a slowly rotating planet a single convection cell would carry air from equator to pole in one loop. On Earth, air moving poleward conserves its angular momentum and therefore accelerates eastward as it approaches the rotation axis, reaching wind speeds that break the flow into eddies well before it gets far. The single cell breaks at about 30 degrees latitude, and the remaining transport is accomplished differently.

The Hadley cell, spanning roughly the equator to 30 degrees, rises where intense equatorial heating and converging trade winds meet along the Intertropical Convergence Zone, a band of persistent deep thunderstorms that migrates seasonally, following the zone of maximum heating north in the boreal summer and south in the austral. Rising air cools, loses its moisture as the tropical rains, and flows poleward aloft as dry air that subsides near 30 degrees. Descending air warms by compression and its relative humidity collapses, which is why the great subtropical desert belt sits almost exactly on that latitude in both hemispheres: the Sahara, the Arabian, the Kalahari, the Atacama and the Australian interior are not coincidences of geography but the surface expression of a circulation. The returning surface flow, deflected westward by rotation, forms the trade winds that carried sailing ships across the Atlantic.

The Ferrel cell, roughly 30 to 60 degrees, is thermally indirect: it rises where the air is cooler and sinks where it is warmer, the opposite of what buoyancy alone would produce. It is not driven by local heating at all but dragged mechanically by the cells on either side and, more importantly, by the travelling depressions and anticyclones of the mid-latitudes, which do most of the actual heat transport there. The Polar cell, 60 to 90 degrees, is a small, cold, thermally direct circulation with sinking air over the poles producing the polar deserts, Antarctica being among the driest places on Earth by precipitation.

Sharp jet streams, narrow ribbons of wind at 9 to 12 kilometres altitude reaching 100 to 200 knots, form at the boundaries where these cells meet and the horizontal temperature contrast is steepest, particularly the polar jet at the Ferrel-Polar boundary. George Hadley described the tropical overturning cell that bears his name in 1735, correctly invoking Earth's rotation to explain the trade winds, though his angular-momentum reasoning was incomplete. The full mathematics of how a rotating reference frame deflects moving air waited a century for Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, who derived it in 1835 while analysing rotating machinery, not weather at all. His result was borrowed into meteorology decades later and is now inseparable from it.

sections.heading: Ocean Currents: The Slower, Deeper Half of the Conveyor
sections.body:
The atmosphere is not the only heat-mover, and below about 30 degrees latitude it is not even the dominant one. Wind stress drags the ocean surface into vast rotating gyres, one in each major basin in each hemisphere, turning clockwise in the north and anticlockwise in the south. Earth's rotation does not merely spin these gyres; it makes them profoundly lopsided. Because the Coriolis parameter increases with latitude, the return flow is squeezed into narrow, fast western boundary currents while the compensating flow spreads lazily across the rest of the basin. The Gulf Stream is the classic case, roughly 100 kilometres wide, moving at up to 2.5 metres per second, and carrying about 30 million cubic metres of water per second past Florida, some thirty times the combined discharge of every river on Earth, with a poleward heat transport on the order of one petawatt. The Kuroshio off Japan, the Agulhas off south-east Africa and the Brazil Current are its counterparts.

Beneath this wind-driven layer, which reaches only a few hundred metres down, a far slower density-driven circulation moves water around the globe on a circuit measured in centuries. Density in seawater depends on both temperature and salinity, hence thermohaline. In the Nordic and Labrador Seas, and around Antarctica, surface water is chilled and made saltier as sea ice forms and rejects brine; it becomes dense enough to sink to the abyss and spread along the ocean floor, eventually upwelling elsewhere over roughly a thousand years. Radiocarbon dating of deep water gives ages of several hundred to over a thousand years, which is how that timescale is known rather than assumed.

Ocean and atmosphere carry roughly comparable shares of the total required poleward heat flux, with the ocean contributing an outsized fraction in the tropics and the atmosphere dominating polewards of about 35 degrees. The ocean also does something the atmosphere cannot: it stores. The heat capacity of the top 3 metres of ocean equals that of the entire atmospheric column above it, and the ocean has absorbed over 90 percent of the excess energy accumulated from human forcing. This is why sea surface temperature records are less noisy than land records, why El Nino events can redistribute enough heat to shift a global annual average by a tenth of a degree, and why the climate system responds to a forcing over decades rather than instantly.
